topics.h: From snowy peaks to sandy deserts and sunny beaches, India packs almost every kind of land into one country. How?
p: India is a land of great geographical diversity: mountains, plains, plateaus, deserts, coasts and islands.

Geographers group India's land into physical regions: the Himalayas in the north, the Northern Plains, the Thar Desert in the west, the Peninsular Plateau in the south, the coastal plains, and the islands.
Each region has its own landforms, rivers, soils, plants and animals, so people's food, homes, clothes and work also differ from region to region.
The Aravalli hills in Rajasthan are among the oldest fold mountains in the world; they are now worn down and much lower than the Himalayas.
This variety of land is one big reason for India's variety of cultures.

ex.q: Why does a farmer in Punjab grow wheat on flat fields, while a family in Ladakh herds yaks and goats?
st: Punjab lies in the Northern Plains, with flat land, fertile soil brought by rivers and plenty of water.
Ladakh lies in the high, cold, dry mountains where farming is difficult and the season is short.
Animals like yaks and goats can survive the cold and give milk, wool and transport.
ex.a: Because the physical region (flat fertile plains versus cold high mountains) shapes how people earn their living.

topics.rl: When you travel by train from Delhi to Chennai, you watch flat plains change to rocky plateau land outside your window.

topics.t: The Himalayas and the Northern Plains
topics.h: 'Himalaya' means 'abode of snow' in Sanskrit. These young, rising mountains feed some of India's mightiest rivers.
p: The Himalayas are young fold mountains. They stretch in an arc along India's northern border.
They have three main parallel ranges: the Greater Himalayas (Himadri, the highest), the Middle Himalayas (Himachal) and the Shiwaliks (the lowest, outer range).
Kangchenjunga, on the border of Sikkim and Nepal, is one of the highest peaks in the world. Mount Everest, the world's highest peak, lies in Nepal.
Snow and glaciers of the Himalayas feed rivers like the Ganga, the Yamuna and the Brahmaputra, which flow all year round.
The Northern Plains lie south of the Himalayas. They were formed by soil laid down by the Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra river systems, and are among the most fertile lands on Earth.

ex.q: Why do the Ganga and Yamuna keep flowing even in the hot, dry month of May?
st: They start from glaciers high in the Himalayas (Gangotri and Yamunotri).
In summer, heat melts snow and ice on the mountains.
This meltwater keeps feeding the rivers even when there is no rain.
ex.a: Because they are fed by melting Himalayan snow and glaciers, they are perennial (year-round) rivers.

topics.rl: Hill towns like Shimla, Mussoorie and Darjeeling are in the Himalayas; families visit them to escape summer heat.

topics.h: The southern half of India is a giant triangle of old rock with hills on both sides and the sea all around.
p: The Peninsular Plateau is a large triangle-shaped tableland made of very old, hard rocks. The Deccan Plateau is its main part.
The Western Ghats (Sahyadri) run along the west edge of the plateau. They are high and continuous, with thick forests and great variety of plants and animals.
The Eastern Ghats run along the east edge. They are lower and broken by rivers like the Mahanadi, Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri, which flow east into the Bay of Bengal.
Coastal plains lie between the Ghats and the sea: a narrow western coast along the Arabian Sea and a wider eastern coast along the Bay of Bengal with big river deltas.
India's islands: Lakshadweep (coral islands in the Arabian Sea) and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands (in the Bay of Bengal). Barren Island in the Andamans has India's only active volcano.

ex.q: Why do most big rivers of the Deccan, like the Godavari and Krishna, flow east into the Bay of Bengal?
st: The Western Ghats are high, so the western side of the plateau is raised.
The plateau slopes gently down towards the east.
Water flows downhill, so the rivers travel east and form deltas on the east coast.
ex.a: Because the Deccan Plateau slopes from west to east.

topics.rl: Kerala's backwaters and Goa's beaches are on the western coastal plain; the Sundarbans mangroves are on the delta of the Ganga and Brahmaputra.

topics.h: Your mother checks the sky before hanging clothes out to dry. She is reading the weather!
p: Weather is the condition of the air (atmosphere) at a particular place and time. It can change within hours or days.
The main elements of weather are temperature, air pressure, humidity, wind (speed and direction) and precipitation (rain, snow or hail).
Temperature tells how hot or cold the air is. Humidity is the amount of water vapour in the air; on a humid day sweat dries slowly and we feel sticky.
Air pressure is the weight of the air pressing down on us. It is lower at higher altitudes, like on mountains.
Wind is moving air. It blows from areas of high pressure towards areas of low pressure.

ex.q: On a hot afternoon in Chennai, wet clothes take longer to dry than on a hot afternoon in Jaipur. Why?
st: Chennai is on the coast, so its air holds a lot of water vapour: humidity is high.
Jaipur is far from the sea and its air is dry: humidity is low.
Water evaporates from clothes slowly when the air is already full of moisture.
ex.a: Because the humidity in Chennai is higher, so evaporation is slower.

topics.rl: Before a cricket match, commentators talk about humidity, wind and the chance of rain because these affect how the ball moves and whether play can continue.

topics.h: A weather station is like a doctor's kit for the sky: each instrument checks one sign of the weather's health.
p: A thermometer measures temperature in degrees Celsius (°C). A maximum-minimum thermometer records the highest and lowest temperature of the day.
A barometer measures air pressure. A falling barometer reading often warns of stormy or rainy weather.
A hygrometer measures humidity. A rain gauge measures rainfall, usually in millimetres (mm).
A wind vane shows the direction the wind is coming from; an anemometer, with spinning cups, measures wind speed.
Instruments are kept in an open space; thermometers are kept in a shaded, airy white box called a Stevenson screen so sunlight does not heat them directly.

ex.q: Neha's school rain gauge collected 12 mm on Monday, 30 mm on Tuesday and 18 mm on Wednesday. What was the total rainfall?
st: Add the three readings: 12 + 30 + 18.
ex.a: 60 mm

topics.rl: The India Meteorological Department (IMD), set up in 1875, runs weather stations across India and gives the forecasts you see on the news.

topics.t: Weather forecasts and why they matter
topics.h: Fishermen in Odisha stay ashore when a cyclone warning comes. A good forecast can keep whole villages safe.
p: A weather forecast is a scientific prediction of the weather for the coming hours or days.
Forecasters use readings from weather stations, weather balloons, radars and satellites, and powerful computers to make predictions.
Farmers use forecasts to decide when to sow, water and harvest. Pilots, sailors and fishermen check forecasts before setting out.
Early warnings of cyclones, heavy rain and heatwaves help people prepare and move to safety in time.
Weather changes from day to day, but the average pattern of weather over many years (usually 30 years or more) is called climate.

ex.q: The forecast says heavy rain will fall tomorrow in a village. What should a farmer who planned to spray fertiliser on his field do?
st: Heavy rain can wash fertiliser off the field.
That would waste money and the fertiliser could flow into ponds and streams.
So it is wiser to wait until the rain has passed.
ex.a: Postpone spraying until after the rain.

topics.rl: Your family's phone weather app and the evening news both use data from the IMD and its satellites.

topics.h: In December, children in Delhi wear sweaters while children in Chennai wear cotton shirts. Same country, same month: why?
p: Climate is the average weather of a place over a long time, usually 30 years or more.
Latitude matters: places nearer the Equator are warmer. The Tropic of Cancer passes through the middle of India, so the south is warmer through the year.
Altitude matters: the higher you go, the cooler it gets. That is why Shimla and Ooty are cool even in summer.
Distance from the sea matters: the sea keeps coastal places like Mumbai moderate, while inland places like Delhi have very hot summers and cold winters.
Winds and mountains matter: the Himalayas block icy winds from Central Asia, and the Western Ghats make moist sea winds drop rain on their western side.

ex.q: Mumbai and Nagpur are at nearly the same latitude. Why are Nagpur's summers hotter and its winters cooler?
st: Mumbai is on the coast; the sea heats and cools slowly, keeping temperatures moderate.
Nagpur is far inland, with no sea nearby to calm the temperature.
So inland Nagpur has bigger swings between summer and winter.
ex.a: Because of distance from the sea: coastal Mumbai has a moderate climate, inland Nagpur has an extreme one.

topics.rl: Hill stations like Munnar, Shimla and Darjeeling became summer getaways because altitude keeps them cool.

topics.h: Every June, people in Kerala watch the sky for the first monsoon clouds. The whole country waits with them!
p: The word 'monsoon' comes from the Arabic word 'mausim', meaning season. Monsoon winds change direction with the seasons.
In summer the land heats up more than the sea. Moist winds from the Indian Ocean blow towards the land as the south-west monsoon, bringing most of India's rain from June to September.
The south-west monsoon usually reaches Kerala around 1 June and then spreads across India in two branches: the Arabian Sea branch and the Bay of Bengal branch.
From late September the monsoon slowly retreats (withdraws). In winter, winds blow from the land towards the sea; the north-east monsoon brings rain to the Tamil Nadu coast from October to December.

Weather scientists usually describe four main seasons: the cold-weather season (winter), the hot-weather season (summer), the south-west monsoon season (June–September) and the season of the retreating monsoon. Traditionally, Indians also speak of six ṛitus: Vasanta, Grīṣhma, Varṣhā, Sharad, Hemanta and Shishira.

ex.q: Why is the arrival of the monsoon so important to Indian farmers?
st: Most of India's yearly rain falls during the south-west monsoon.
Many farmers depend on this rain to sow crops like rice, cotton and maize.
A late or weak monsoon can reduce harvests; a good monsoon fills ponds, wells and reservoirs.
ex.a: Because the monsoon brings most of the rain that crops, wells and rivers depend on.

topics.rl: Festivals like Onam in Kerala and Pola in Maharashtra are linked to the farming calendar shaped by the monsoon.

topics.h: In the same week, a camel may be crossing hot sand in Jaisalmer while a yak walks over frozen ground in Ladakh!
p: Because of its size, landforms and position, India has many climate regions.
Hot and dry regions, like the Thar Desert, get very little rain and have very hot summers. Hot, dry winds called 'loo' blow across the northern plains in May and June.
Very wet regions, like the Kerala coast, the Western Ghats and the north-east, get heavy rain. Mawsynram and Sohra (Cherrapunji) in Meghalaya are among the wettest places on Earth.
Cold mountain regions, like Ladakh, have long freezing winters. Ladakh is a cold desert because it gets very little rain or snow.
Climate shapes daily life: thick-walled homes and loose cotton clothes in hot places, sloping roofs where rain is heavy, and woollen clothes in cold mountains.

ex.q: Why do many houses in Meghalaya and Kerala have steeply sloping roofs, while old houses in Rajasthan often have flat roofs?
st: Meghalaya and Kerala get very heavy rain.
Sloping roofs let rainwater run off quickly so it does not collect and leak.
Rajasthan gets little rain, so flat roofs are fine and can even be used for sleeping on hot nights.
ex.a: Sloping roofs suit heavy-rain regions; flat roofs suit dry regions.

topics.rl: Look at what people wear and how they build homes on a family trip; you are seeing how people adapt to climate.

topics.h: Imagine a group of families settling beside a river, clearing land and calling it home. That's how a janapada began!
p: After the great Harappan cities declined (after about 1900 BCE), people in northern India lived mostly in villages for many centuries.
The Vedas are the oldest texts of India. The Rigveda is the oldest of the four Vedas (Rig, Sama, Yajur and Atharva). They tell us about the life, beliefs and prayers of the people who composed them.
A 'jana' was a people or clan. 'Janapada' means 'the place where a jana set its foot', that is, a territory where a people settled.
Janapadas had their own rulers or councils. Early Vedic texts mention assemblies called the sabhā and the samiti where important matters were discussed.
Over time, some janapadas grew larger and stronger by adding land, people and wealth.

ex.q: A word is made of 'jana' (people) and 'pada' (foot). Why is 'janapada' a good name for a settled territory?
st: 'Pada' means foot, so 'janapada' is where the people placed their foot.
Placing one's foot somewhere suggests settling down in that place.
So the word describes land where a people settled.
ex.a: Because it means 'the land where a people set foot and settled'.

topics.rl: Many Indian place names still keep old meanings; studying such words is one way historians learn about the past.

topics.h: Around 2,600 years ago, sixteen 'great janapadas' stretched across northern India, from Gandhara to Anga.
p: By about the 6th century BCE, there were sixteen mahājanapadas ('great janapadas'). Buddhist and Jain texts list them, though their lists differ slightly.
Examples with their capitals: Magadha (Rājagṛiha), Kosala (Shrāvastī), Avanti (Ujjayinī), Vatsa (Kaushāmbī), Gandhāra (Takshashilā), Kāshī (Vārāṇasī), Anga (Champā) and Vajji (Vaishālī).
Many mahājanapadas were ruled by kings. Some, like the Vajji and the Malla, were gaṇas or saṅghas, where power was shared by a group, and decisions were discussed in assemblies.
Mahājanapadas had capital cities, often protected by strong walls and moats, and collected taxes to pay for armies and officials.
They often fought one another for land and power. In time, Magadha became the most powerful.

ex.q: A mahājanapada was ruled by an assembly of many leaders who discussed and decided matters together. Was it a monarchy?
st: In a monarchy, one king rules and the throne usually passes in the family.
Here power was shared by a group in an assembly.
This matches a gaṇa or saṅgha.
ex.a: No. It was a gaṇa or saṅgha, where power was shared by a group.

topics.rl: Ujjain (Ujjayinī), Varanasi and Patna (Pāṭaliputra) are still busy cities today, showing how old some Indian cities are.

topics.h: After a long gap following the Harappan age, cities appeared again in the Ganga plains, buzzing with traders, craftspeople and markets.
p: From about the 6th century BCE, new cities grew in the Ganga plains. Historians often call this the 'second urbanisation'; the Harappan cities were the first.
Iron tools like axes and ploughs helped people clear forests and grow more food. Extra food could feed people in cities who did not farm.
Cities like Rājagṛiha, Shrāvastī, Kaushāmbī, Vārāṇasī and Ujjayinī had fortification walls and moats, markets and crafts workshops.
Trade grew. Punch-marked coins, mostly of silver, were used to buy and sell. A shiny pottery called Northern Black Polished Ware is found at many of these sites.
Craftspeople and traders formed groups called shreṇīs (guilds). This was also the age of the Buddha and Mahāvīra.

ex.q: Why did the use of iron tools help cities to grow?
st: Iron axes cleared thick forests of the Ganga plains more easily.
Iron ploughs helped farmers grow more grain.
More food meant some people could live in towns as traders, craftspeople and officials.
ex.a: Iron tools increased farm output, and extra food could support city people who did not farm.

topics.rl: Today's traders' associations are a bit like the shreṇīs of ancient times, where people in the same craft or trade worked together.

topics.h: Out of sixteen great janapadas, one grew into the heart of India's first big empire. What made Magadha so special?
p: Magadha lay in the fertile middle Ganga plains, in present-day Bihar. Its farms grew plenty of rice and other crops.
It had rich iron-ore deposits nearby (in present-day Jharkhand), so it could make strong tools and weapons.
Its forests supplied elephants for the army and timber for building. Rivers like the Ganga and Son helped transport and trade.
Its early capital Rājagṛiha was protected by hills; the later capital Pāṭaliputra (today's Patna) stood on the Ganga.
Strong rulers expanded it: Bimbisāra and Ajātashatru (Haryanka dynasty), then the Shishunāgas and the very wealthy Nandas.

ex.q: List two ways in which geography helped Magadha become powerful.
st: Fertile land gave surplus food and taxes.
Nearby iron ore gave tools and weapons.
Forests gave elephants for the army; rivers helped trade and the movement of soldiers.
ex.a: Any two: fertile land, iron ore, forests with elephants, and rivers for transport.

topics.rl: When you visit Rajgir or Patna in Bihar, you are walking where Magadha's capitals stood more than 2,000 years ago.

topics.h: A young man and his wise teacher together built one of the largest empires India had ever seen.
p: Around 321 BCE, Chandragupta Maurya, guided by his teacher Chāṇakya (also called Kauṭilya), overthrew the Nandas and founded the Mauryan Empire, with Pāṭaliputra as its capital.
The Arthashāstra, linked with Kauṭilya, is a book on statecraft: how to run a kingdom, collect taxes, keep spies, manage trade and protect people.
The Arthashāstra describes seven 'limbs' (saptāṅga) of a state: the king, ministers, territory with its people, fort, treasury, army and allies.
Megasthenes, a Greek ambassador sent by Seleucus, lived at Chandragupta's court and wrote a book called Indica, which survives only in quotes by later writers.
Chandragupta's son Bindusāra and grandson Ashoka ruled after him. At its peak, the empire covered most of the subcontinent.

ex.q: The Arthashāstra lists the treasury as one 'limb' of the state. Why would a kingdom be weak without it?
st: A treasury stores the wealth collected from taxes.
This money pays soldiers, officials and builders of roads and forts.
Without it, the army and government could not work.
ex.a: Because without money the king cannot pay the army and officials who protect and run the kingdom.

topics.rl: Chanakyapuri, a well-known area of New Delhi where many embassies are located, is named after Chāṇakya.

topics.h: After winning a terrible war, a mighty emperor decided to conquer hearts instead of lands.
p: Ashoka, grandson of Chandragupta, fought a war against Kalinga (in present-day Odisha). The great loss of life in this war filled him with sorrow.
After Kalinga, Ashoka gave up wars of conquest and followed dhamma: kindness, truthfulness, respect for elders and teachers, care for animals, and respect for all faiths.
He spread his message through edicts carved on rocks and pillars, mostly in Prakrit and in the Brāhmī script. In 1837 James Prinsep deciphered the Brāhmī script, so we can read them today.
Ashoka set up hospitals for people and animals, had wells dug and trees planted along roads, and sent messengers to other lands. His son Mahinda (Mahendra) took Buddhism to Sri Lanka.
The Lion Capital of his pillar at Sarnath is India's National Emblem, and the chakra on our national flag, with 24 spokes, comes from Ashoka's pillars.

ex.q: Ashoka wrote his edicts on rocks and pillars along roads and near towns, in the people's language. Why?
st: He wanted ordinary people, not just scholars, to learn about dhamma.
Rocks and pillars last a very long time and are seen by travellers.
Using Prakrit, a language people spoke, made the message easy to understand.
ex.a: So that many people could read or hear his message and it would last for a long time.

topics.rl: Indian rupee notes and coins carry the Lion Capital from Sarnath, and the Ashoka Chakra sits at the centre of the Indian flag.

topics.t: After the Mauryas: new kingdoms in India
topics.h: When a huge empire breaks up, many new kingdoms rise to fill the space. That's what happened after the Mauryas.
p: Around 185 BCE, the last Mauryan ruler, Bṛihadratha, was overthrown by his general Pushyamitra Shunga, who started the Shunga dynasty. The Kāṇvas later followed the Shungas.

In the Deccan, the Sātavāhanas became powerful. Their capital was Pratiṣhṭhāna (Paithan) on the Godavari. Many Sātavāhana kings were named after their mothers, such as Gautamīputra Sātakarṇi, 'son of Gautamī'.
In Kalinga, King Khāravela became powerful some time after the Mauryas. His Hāthīgumphā inscription in the Udayagiri hills near Bhubaneswar records his deeds; he was a follower of Jainism.
In the far south, the Cheras, Cholas and Pāṇḍyas ruled Tamilakam. Early Tamil poems called Sangam literature describe their kings, poets, farmers and ports.
Historians call this period an 'age of reorganisation' because power was divided among many kingdoms, while trade and culture kept growing.

ex.q: The king's name 'Gautamīputra Sātakarṇi' tells us something. What does 'Gautamīputra' show?
st: 'Putra' means son.
'Gautamī' is the name of his mother.
So the king was known as the son of Gautamī.
ex.a: It shows that Sātavāhana kings were often named after their mothers.

topics.rl: The Hāthīgumphā ('elephant cave') inscription and the Udayagiri–Khandagiri caves near Bhubaneswar can still be visited today.

topics.h: Greek kings who discussed Buddhism, and Central Asian rulers who issued gold coins: north-west India was a meeting place of peoples.
p: Indo-Greek kings ruled parts of the north-west. The most famous, Menander (Milinda), is remembered in a Buddhist text, the Milinda-pañha ('Questions of Milinda'), where he asks the monk Nāgasena about the Buddha's teachings.
Heliodorus, a Greek ambassador, set up a pillar at Besnagar near Vidisha in honour of Vāsudeva (Krishna).
The Shakas came from Central Asia. The Shaka ruler Rudradāman's inscription at Junagadh (Girnar), in Sanskrit, records the repair of the Sudarshana lake.
The Kushānas built a large kingdom; their greatest ruler, Kanishka, supported Buddhism. Their capitals included Puruṣhapura (Peshawar) and Mathurā.
Many newcomers adopted Indian names, languages and faiths, and became part of Indian society.

ex.q: A Greek ambassador set up a pillar honouring an Indian deity. What does this tell us about the time?
st: Heliodorus came from a Greek kingdom, yet he honoured Vāsudeva.
This shows that newcomers were adopting Indian beliefs.
It suggests the period was one of mixing and exchange of cultures.
ex.a: That people from outside were becoming part of Indian culture and faith.

topics.rl: The Government Museum in Mathura displays a Kushāna-period statue of Kanishka.

topics.h: Indian pepper was so valued by Roman traders that it is often called 'black gold'. Ships crossed the ocean to buy it!
p: Trade grew by land and sea. The Silk Route linked China, Central Asia, India and the Mediterranean world; Kushāna rule helped trade along these routes.
Traders used the monsoon winds to sail across the Arabian Sea. Spices (especially pepper), cotton cloth, gems and ivory went west.
Roman coins have been found in south India, and Arikamedu near Puducherry was an important trading site. Muziris on the Kerala coast was a famous port.
Art flourished. Gandhāra art, influenced by Greek styles, made Buddha images with wavy hair and flowing robes; Mathurā art used local red sandstone.
The gateways (toraṇas) of the Great Stupa at Sanchi, with their beautiful carvings, belong largely to this age. Sanskrit, Prakrit and Tamil literature also flourished.

ex.q: Many Roman gold and silver coins have been dug up in Tamil Nadu and Kerala. What does this tell historians?
st: Roman traders must have paid for goods with these coins.
So there was active trade between south India and the Roman world.
The goods they bought were mainly spices, cloth and gems.
ex.a: That south India had busy sea trade with the Roman world.

topics.rl: Kerala is still one of India's major pepper-growing regions, carrying on a spice trade that is over 2,000 years old.

topics.ch: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
topics.h: A king who played the veena on his coins and a court poet who carved his praises on Ashoka's pillar: welcome to the Gupta age!
p: The Gupta dynasty became powerful in the early 4th century CE. Chandragupta I, who married the Licchavi princess Kumāradevī, made the kingdom strong around 320 CE.

His son Samudragupta won many wars. His court poet Hariṣheṇa composed a praśasti (praise poem) that was carved on the Ashokan pillar at Prayāgarāja (Prayagraj). Some of his gold coins show him playing the veena.
Chandragupta II (also called Vikramāditya) defeated the Shakas of western India. The Chinese Buddhist pilgrim Faxian (Fa-hien) travelled in India during his reign.
Kumāragupta I is linked with the founding of the great university at Nālandā. Skandagupta defended the empire against the Hūṇas from Central Asia.
The Guptas issued many beautiful gold coins. Their rule is remembered as a time of great creativity in science, art and literature.

ex.q: Samudragupta's achievements are known from a poem carved on an older Ashokan pillar. Why are such praśastis useful but also to be read carefully?
st: A praśasti gives names of places, kings and wars of the time, which is valuable information.
But it was written by a court poet to praise the king.
So historians compare it with coins and other sources before accepting every claim.
ex.a: They are useful records, but as praise poems they may exaggerate, so they are checked against other evidence.

topics.rl: The pillar with both Ashoka's edicts and Samudragupta's praśasti can be seen inside the Allahabad Fort in Prayagraj.

topics.ch: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
topics.t: Science and mathematics in the Gupta age
topics.h: About 1,500 years ago, a 23-year-old Indian astronomer explained eclipses with shadows, not demons!
p: Āryabhaṭa wrote the Āryabhaṭīya in 499 CE. He stated that the Earth rotates on its axis, which makes the stars seem to move across the sky.
Āryabhaṭa explained that eclipses happen because of the shadows of the Earth and the Moon. He gave a very close value of pi (π), about 3.1416.
Varāhamihira wrote the Bṛihat Saṁhitā, a great book on astronomy, weather, plants, gems, building and much more.
Indian mathematicians used the decimal place-value system, which later spread to the world through Arab scholars.
Metal-workers made the Iron Pillar, now in Mehrauli, Delhi. More than 1,500 years later it has hardly rusted, showing their skill in metallurgy.

ex.q: Āryabhaṭa said that the stars seem to move from east to west because the Earth rotates. How can you test this idea with a simple observation?
st: Sit in a moving train and look at trees outside.
The trees seem to move backward, though it is the train that moves.
In the same way, the Earth's rotation makes the sky seem to turn around us.
ex.a: Like trees seeming to move past a moving train, the sky seems to move because the Earth itself rotates.

topics.rl: India's first satellite, launched in 1975, was named Aryabhata in honour of the great astronomer.

topics.ch: The Gupta Era: An Age of Tireless Creativity
topics.t: Art and literature of the Gupta age
topics.h: A cloud carrying a love message across India, and cave walls glowing with paintings: Gupta-age art still amazes the world.
p: Kālidāsa was a great Sanskrit poet and playwright. His works include the play Abhijñāna-Shākuntalam and the poem Meghadūta, in which a cloud carries a message.
Many of the famous paintings in the Ajanta caves in Maharashtra were made in the 5th century CE. They show scenes from the Buddha's life and stories (Jātakas) with rich colours.
Some of the earliest stone temples were built in this age, such as the Dashāvatāra temple at Deogarh in Uttar Pradesh. The Udayagiri caves near Vidisha have a huge carving of Varāha.
Nālandā grew into a great centre of learning where students studied many subjects.
Sanskrit became a major language of literature, learning and royal inscriptions.

ex.q: In the Meghadūta, a cloud flies over mountains, rivers and towns to carry a message. What can a historian learn from such a poem?
st: The poem names and describes places, rivers and mountains along the route.
So it shows what people of that time knew about India's geography.
It also shows the beauty of Sanskrit poetry of that age.
ex.a: It shows the geography people knew and the high skill of Sanskrit poetry at that time.

topics.rl: Ajanta's caves near Aurangabad (Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar) are a UNESCO World Heritage Site, visited by people from all over the world.

topics.h: In some villages, no one cuts a single branch in the forest patch near the temple. The trees are protected because the land is sacred!
p: Across India, people see certain rivers, mountains, forests, trees and lakes as sacred. This web of sacred places is called sacred geography.
Rivers such as the Ganga, Yamuna, Narmada, Godavari and Kaveri are honoured as sacred. Some devotees walk the Narmada parikramā, a long journey along both banks of the river.
Mountains like Kailash in Tibet are sacred to many traditions, including Hindus, Buddhists and Jains.

Sacred groves are patches of forest protected by local communities because they are linked to a deity. They have different names: devrai in Maharashtra, kāvu in Kerala, sarnā in Jharkhand and orans in Rajasthan.
Trees like the peepal and banyan and plants like tulsi are respected in many homes. Treating nature as sacred has often helped protect it.

ex.q: A sacred grove in Maharashtra has very old trees and rare plants that have disappeared from the land around it. Why?
st: The local community believes the grove belongs to a deity.
By tradition, people do not cut trees or hunt there.
So plants and animals in the grove have been protected for a very long time.
ex.a: Because the community's belief that the grove is sacred has protected it from cutting and hunting.

topics.rl: Many schools and nature clubs now study sacred groves, because they are like small natural museums of plants and animals.

topics.h: Every year, lakhs of warkaris walk for days, singing, to Pandharpur in Maharashtra. A pilgrimage can be a journey of joy!
p: A tīrtha is a sacred place of pilgrimage. The word originally meant a ford, a place to cross a river.
The Char Dhām are Badrinath (north), Dwarka (west), Puri (east) and Rameswaram (south). By tradition they are linked with Ādi Shaṅkarāchārya, and together they connect all corners of India.
The twelve Jyotirliṅgas, sacred to devotees of Shiva, are spread across India, from Somnath in Gujarat to Rameswaram in Tamil Nadu and Kedarnath in Uttarakhand.
The Kumbh Melā is held by turn at Prayagraj, Haridwar, Ujjain and Nashik; each place hosts it about once every 12 years. UNESCO lists it as an intangible cultural heritage of humanity.
In the Pandharpur Wārī, warkaris walk with the pālkhīs (palanquins) of saints Dnyāneshwar and Tukārām to the Vitthala temple at Pandharpur.

ex.q: A family from Kashi (Varanasi) takes Ganga water on a pilgrimage to Rameswaram in the far south. What does this tradition show?
st: Kashi is in the north, Rameswaram in the far south.
Carrying water from one sacred place to another links them.
Such journeys connected people from different regions, languages and foods.
ex.a: That pilgrimages tied distant parts of India together into one sacred landscape.

topics.rl: During a yatra, pilgrims meet people from many states, try new foods and hear new languages: travel itself becomes learning.

topics.h: A Buddhist monk at Bodh Gaya, a Jain family climbing Palitana's steps, and Sikh pilgrims at the Golden Temple: India's sacred map belongs to everyone.
p: Buddhist pilgrims visit four main places linked with the Buddha's life: Lumbini (birth, in Nepal), Bodh Gaya (enlightenment), Sarnath (first sermon) and Kushinagar (passing away).
Jain pilgrims climb the Shatruñjaya hills at Palitana in Gujarat and visit Sammed Shikhar in Jharkhand. Shravanabelagola in Karnataka has the great statue of Bāhubali (Gommateshwara).
The Harmandir Sahib (Golden Temple) in Amritsar is the holiest gurdwara of the Sikhs; its langar serves free meals to all visitors.
Sufi shrines (dargāhs), such as the dargāh of Khwāja Moinuddin Chishtī at Ajmer, are visited by people of many faiths.
Christian pilgrims visit places like the Basilica of Bom Jesus in Goa and the Basilica at Velankanni in Tamil Nadu. Visiting each other's sacred places shows India's spirit of respect and sharing.

ex.q: Why do people of different faiths often visit the same shrine, such as the dargāh at Ajmer?
st: Many people visit to pray for wishes, peace or thanks.
The shrine welcomes everyone, whatever their faith.
This sharing builds respect and friendship between communities.
ex.a: Because such shrines are open to all, and people of many faiths share a respect for them.

topics.rl: When you eat at a gurdwara langar, you sit on the floor with everyone, rich or poor, of any faith: a simple lesson in equality.

topics.ch: From the Rulers to the Ruled: Types of Governments
topics.t: Why governments, and rule by monarchs
topics.h: Imagine a cricket match with no umpire and no rules. Every country needs someone to make and run the rules: a government.
p: A government makes laws, keeps order, protects the country, settles disputes and provides services like schools, hospitals and roads.
Governments differ in who holds power, how rulers are chosen and how much say the people have.
In a monarchy, a king or queen (a monarch) is head of the state, and the position usually passes down in the family.

In an absolute monarchy, the monarch holds almost all power. In a constitutional monarchy, the monarch's powers are limited by a constitution and an elected parliament makes the laws. The United Kingdom, Japan and Bhutan have constitutional monarchies.
For much of history, most kingdoms in India and the world were monarchies, though some ancient Indian gaṇas shared power among a group.

ex.q: Bhutan has a king, and also an elected parliament that makes laws under a constitution. What kind of government is this?
st: There is a monarch, so it is a monarchy.
But laws are made by an elected parliament under a constitution.
So the king's powers are limited by the constitution.
ex.a: A constitutional monarchy.

topics.rl: When your class elects a monitor instead of a teacher simply choosing one, you are seeing a small difference in how leaders can be chosen.

topics.ch: From the Rulers to the Ruled: Types of Governments
topics.h: India holds the largest elections in the world. Every adult citizen's vote counts the same, from a farmer in Bihar to a scientist in Bengaluru.
p: In a democracy, people choose their rulers through free and fair elections. Abraham Lincoln described democracy as 'government of the people, by the people, for the people'.

In a direct democracy, citizens themselves vote on laws, as in ancient Athens. In a representative democracy, citizens elect representatives who make laws for them. India is a representative democracy.
India gives universal adult franchise: every citizen aged 18 or above can vote, whatever their religion, caste, gender, wealth or education.
The Election Commission of India, set up on 25 January 1950, conducts elections. That date is celebrated as National Voters' Day.
Voters use Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs), and an ink mark on the finger shows that a person has voted.

ex.q: Ravi turned 18 last month. His grandfather never went to school. His neighbour is very rich. Who among them can vote in India?
st: India has universal adult franchise.
Every citizen aged 18 or above can vote, regardless of education or wealth.
Ravi is 18, and the grandfather and neighbour are adults too.
ex.a: All three can vote, if they are Indian citizens registered as voters.

topics.rl: On polling day, schools often become polling booths, and you may see your parents return with the ink mark on their finger.

topics.ch: From the Rulers to the Ruled: Types of Governments
topics.t: Dictatorship, theocracy and how governments differ
topics.h: What if one person made all the rules and no one was allowed to question them? That's the danger of a dictatorship.
p: In a dictatorship, one person (or a small group) holds all power and is not chosen through free and fair elections. People usually cannot criticise the ruler freely.
In an oligarchy, a small group of powerful people, such as the very rich or military leaders, rules.
In a theocracy, religious leaders rule, or the laws are based on the rules of one religion.
Governments can be compared by asking: Who holds power? How are rulers chosen? Can they be removed peacefully? Do people have rights and freedom of speech?
In a democracy, rulers can be changed peacefully through elections, and there are courts, a free press and rights to protect citizens.

ex.q: A ruler took power without an election, bans newspapers that criticise him and has stayed in power for 30 years. Which type of government is this most like?
st: He was not chosen through an election.
He does not allow criticism.
Power stays with one person who cannot be changed peacefully.
ex.a: A dictatorship.

topics.rl: In a school, a class where everyone votes on the picnic place is like a democracy; one where the class bully decides everything is like a dictatorship.

topics.ch: The Constitution of India — An Introduction
topics.h: India's Constitution was not written in a day. Hundreds of members debated it for nearly three years before signing it by hand!
p: A constitution is the basic rulebook of a country. It sets up the government, divides its powers and protects the rights of citizens.
The Constituent Assembly, which wrote India's Constitution, first met on 9 December 1946. Dr Rajendra Prasad was elected its President.
Dr B. R. Ambedkar chaired the Drafting Committee, which prepared the draft. He is often called the chief architect of the Constitution.
The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 (now Constitution Day, or Samvidhan Divas) and came into force on 26 January 1950 (Republic Day). It took nearly three years to make.

The Assembly included members from many regions and communities, including 15 women such as Sarojini Naidu, Hansa Mehta, Durgabai Deshmukh and Ammu Swaminathan. The original copies were handwritten and decorated by artists led by Nandalal Bose.

ex.q: Why was 26 January chosen as the day the Constitution would come into force?
st: On 26 January 1930, Indian freedom fighters had pledged to work for Pūrṇa Swarāj (complete independence).
Leaders wanted to honour that pledge.
So the Constitution, adopted in November 1949, was brought into force on 26 January 1950.
ex.a: To honour the Pūrṇa Swarāj pledge made on 26 January 1930.

topics.rl: Every year on Republic Day, the parade in New Delhi celebrates the day our Constitution came into force; schools celebrate Constitution Day on 26 November.

topics.ch: The Constitution of India — An Introduction
topics.h: The Preamble is like the first page of a promise: it tells us who made the Constitution and what kind of country India wants to be.
p: The Preamble begins with 'We, the people of India', showing that the Constitution draws its power from the people.
It declares India to be a Sovereign, Socialist, Secular, Democratic Republic. The words 'socialist' and 'secular' were added in 1976 by the 42nd Amendment.

Sovereign: India makes its own decisions. Secular: the State treats all religions equally and has no official religion. Democratic: people elect their government. Republic: the head of the state is elected, not a hereditary ruler.

It promises citizens Justice (social, economic and political), Liberty (of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship), Equality (of status and opportunity) and Fraternity (a feeling of brotherhood and sisterhood).
Fraternity assures the dignity of every individual and the unity and integrity of the nation.

ex.q: India's President is elected, not born into the job. Which word in the Preamble does this fact show?
st: A republic is a country where the head of the state is elected.
India's head of state, the President, is elected.
So India is a republic, not a monarchy.
ex.a: Republic.

topics.rl: Many schools have students read the Preamble aloud in the morning assembly to remember these shared values.

topics.ch: The Constitution of India — An Introduction
topics.t: Rights, duties and the spirit of the Constitution
topics.h: Rights are like the shield the Constitution gives you; duties are what you give back to the country.
p: The Constitution gives every citizen Fundamental Rights: the Right to Equality, Right to Freedom, Right against Exploitation, Right to Freedom of Religion, Cultural and Educational Rights, and the Right to Constitutional Remedies.
The Right to Constitutional Remedies lets a citizen go to court if their rights are violated. Dr Ambedkar called it the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution.
Fundamental Duties were added in 1976. They include respecting the Constitution, the national flag and the national anthem, protecting the environment, and protecting public property.

The Constitution of India is the longest written constitution in the world. It can be amended (changed) by Parliament, but in the Kesavananda Bharati case (1973) the Supreme Court held that its basic structure cannot be changed.
It sets up a federal system with a Union government and State governments, and a separate, independent judiciary.

ex.q: A child aged 12 is made to work all day in a factory instead of going to school. Which Fundamental Right protects this child?
st: Making a young child work in a factory is exploitation.
The Constitution bans employing children below 14 in factories, mines and hazardous work.
This is part of the Right against Exploitation.
ex.a: The Right against Exploitation.

topics.rl: When you keep your park clean or do not scribble on a public bus, you are doing a Fundamental Duty: protecting public property and the environment.

topics.h: Imagine trying to buy a pencil with a coconut! Before money, that's how people traded.
p: Barter is the direct exchange of goods or services for other goods or services, without using money.
Barter works only if each person has what the other wants. This is called the 'double coincidence of wants', and it is often hard to find.
Barter has other problems too: there is no common measure of value (how many pots for one goat?), some goods cannot be divided (half a cow is no use), and many goods spoil if stored.
Barter was common in early societies, and some barter still happens in villages, at fairs and between friends.
These problems led people to look for something that everyone would accept in exchange: money.

ex.q: A potter wants rice. The rice farmer does not need pots; he needs cloth. Why is the potter stuck, and how could money help?
st: The potter has pots, but the farmer does not want pots: there is no double coincidence of wants.
The potter would first have to find someone who wants pots and has cloth, then trade again.
With money, the potter can sell pots to anyone, and use the money to buy rice.
ex.a: Barter fails without a double coincidence of wants; money solves it because everyone accepts it.

topics.rl: When you swap a sandwich for a friend's paratha at lunch, you are bartering!

topics.h: Shells, salt, cattle, metal and paper: money has worn many costumes through history!
p: Before coins, people used commodity money: useful items like grain, cattle, salt and cowrie shells that many people accepted. Cowrie shells were used in parts of India for a very long time.
Some of the world's earliest coins were made in Lydia (in present-day Turkey) around the 7th century BCE.
In India, the earliest coins are punch-marked coins, mostly of silver, from around the 6th century BCE. Symbols were punched onto metal pieces.

Later Indian rulers issued coins with names and portraits: Indo-Greek kings, Kushānas and Guptas (famous for gold coins). In the 16th century, Sher Shah Suri issued a silver coin called the 'rupiya', from which the word 'rupee' comes.
China was the first country to use paper money. Paper notes are light and easy to carry, and their value comes from the trust that people and the government place in them.

ex.q: Why would a trader prefer a silver coin to a bag of grain as money?
st: Grain is heavy and can spoil or be eaten by pests.
A silver coin is small, lasts a long time and is easy to carry.
Coins of fixed weight are easy to count and compare.
ex.a: Coins are durable, portable and easy to count, unlike grain.

topics.rl: Museums like the National Museum in New Delhi display ancient Indian coins, from punch-marked silver to Gupta gold.

topics.t: Money today: the rupee, RBI and digital payments
topics.h: A ₹10 note, a coin, a card and a phone scan can all pay for the same samosa. How does it all work?
p: Money has four main functions: a medium of exchange (we use it to buy and sell), a measure of value (prices are in rupees), a store of value (we can save it) and a standard of deferred payment (loans can be repaid later in money).
The Reserve Bank of India (RBI), set up on 1 April 1935, is India's central bank. It issues currency notes; the Government of India issues coins and the ₹1 note.
The rupee symbol ₹ was adopted in 2010. It was designed by D. Udaya Kumar and combines the Devanagari 'र' and the Roman 'R'.
Today many people pay digitally, with cards, net banking and UPI (Unified Payments Interface), launched in 2016, which lets money move instantly between bank accounts using a phone.
Digital payments are fast and convenient, but we must keep our PIN and OTP secret and never share them with anyone.

ex.q: Aditi saved ₹500 from her birthday gifts and spent it a year later on books. Which function of money does saving show?
st: She did not spend the money immediately.
She kept its value for a future purchase.
Holding value over time is the store-of-value function.
ex.a: Store of value.

topics.rl: At the vegetable market, many sellers now display a QR code so you can pay by UPI with a phone.

topics.h: A weekly haat under a banyan tree, a busy sabzi mandi, a shiny mall and a shopping app: all of them are markets!
p: A market is any place or arrangement where buyers and sellers meet to exchange goods and services. It does not have to be a physical place.
Markets by place: weekly markets (haats) that come up on a fixed day, neighbourhood shops, shopping complexes and malls, and online markets on websites and apps.
Wholesale markets (like big mandis) sell goods in large quantities to traders. Retail markets sell in small quantities to the final buyer, the consumer.

Markets by competition: in a competitive market, there are many sellers of similar goods (like a vegetable market). In a monopoly, there is only one seller. In an oligopoly, a few big sellers control the market.
Weekly haats are cheaper for many families because sellers have low costs: they do not pay rent for permanent shops.

ex.q: A town has only one company that supplies electricity, and people cannot buy it from anyone else. What kind of market is this?
st: Count the sellers: only one.
Buyers have no other choice of seller.
A market with a single seller is a monopoly.
ex.a: A monopoly.

topics.rl: Before Diwali, your family may buy diyas at a local haat, sweets from a neighbourhood shop and clothes from a mall or an app.

topics.h: A tomato travels from a farm to a mandi, to a trader, to a shop and finally to your kitchen. Many hands help it on the way!
p: Between producers and consumers there are often intermediaries (middlemen) such as wholesalers and retailers. They transport, store and sell goods, and each adds to the final price.
In many states, farmers sell crops at regulated markets (mandis) run under Agricultural Produce Market Committees (APMCs).

Buyers are called consumers. Consumers have rights: to safety, to be informed, to choose, to be heard, to seek redressal (remedy) and to consumer education. The Consumer Protection Act, 2019, protects these rights.
Quality marks help consumers: ISI on many industrial products, AGMARK on farm products like honey and spices, and the BIS Hallmark on gold jewellery.
A seller cannot charge more than the MRP (maximum retail price) printed on a packet. Consumers can complain to consumer commissions or call the National Consumer Helpline (1915).

ex.q: Raju bought a packet of chips marked MRP ₹20, but the shopkeeper charged ₹25. What should Raju know?
st: MRP is the maximum retail price allowed.
Charging ₹25 is more than the MRP, which is not allowed.
Raju can refuse to pay extra and can complain, for example to the National Consumer Helpline.
ex.a: He should pay no more than ₹20 and can complain if overcharged.

topics.rl: Next time you buy honey or a pressure cooker at home, look for the AGMARK or ISI mark on the label.

topics.h: When mangoes first arrive in April they are costly; by June, when carts are full of mangoes, prices fall. Why?
p: Demand is the quantity of a good that buyers are willing and able to buy at different prices.
Law of demand: when the price of a good rises, people usually buy less of it; when the price falls, they buy more (other things staying the same).
Supply is the quantity that sellers are willing to sell at different prices. Law of supply: when the price rises, sellers usually offer more; when it falls, they offer less.
The price at which the quantity demanded equals the quantity supplied is called the equilibrium (market) price.
If supply is very large compared with demand, prices fall; if demand is much larger than supply, prices rise. Weather, festivals and seasons can shift demand and supply.

ex.q: A fruit seller finds: at ₹40 a kg people buy 50 kg of mangoes a day; at ₹60, 35 kg; at ₹80, 20 kg; at ₹100, 10 kg. What pattern does this show?
st: As the price goes up from ₹40 to ₹100, the quantity bought goes down from 50 kg to 10 kg.
Higher price, lower quantity demanded.
This is the law of demand.
ex.a: The law of demand: higher price, less is bought.

topics.rl: Before Raksha Bandhan, rakhi prices rise because demand jumps for a few days; after the festival, leftover rakhis are sold cheaply.

topics.t: The long history of Indian farming
topics.h: Farmers in the Indian subcontinent have been growing crops for thousands of years. Some of their ideas are still used today!
p: Mehrgarh, at the foot of the Bolan Pass (in present-day Pakistan), is one of the earliest known farming villages in the subcontinent. People there grew wheat and barley and kept cattle, sheep and goats.
Harappan farmers grew wheat, barley, pulses and cotton. Remains of a ploughed field have been found at Kalibangan in Rajasthan.
Ancient texts such as the Kṛiṣhi-Parāshara give advice on rain, seeds, ploughing and caring for cattle. The Vṛikṣhāyurveda deals with the care of plants and trees.
The Kallaṇai (Grand Anicut) across the Kaveri, built by the Chola king Karikāla about 2,000 years ago, is one of the oldest water-diversion structures in the world still in use.

In the 1960s, the Green Revolution brought high-yielding varieties of wheat and rice, with more irrigation and fertilisers, greatly increasing harvests, especially in Punjab and Haryana. Dr M. S. Swaminathan was a leading scientist of this effort.

ex.q: The Kallaṇai on the Kaveri has been used for about 2,000 years. What does this tell us about early Tamil farmers?
st: The dam diverts river water into channels for fields.
Building something that lasts 2,000 years needs great engineering skill.
So early farmers and rulers understood rivers and water management very well.
ex.a: That they had advanced knowledge of water management and engineering for farming.

topics.rl: In many villages, farmers still read the sky, winds and birds to predict rain, carrying forward knowledge from very old times.

topics.h: Rice loves the rainy season, while wheat likes cool winters. Indian farmers plan their year around crop seasons.
p: India has three main crop seasons. Kharif crops are sown with the monsoon (June–July) and harvested in September–October: rice, maize, cotton, jowar, bajra, groundnut and soybean.
Rabi crops are sown in winter (October–December) and harvested in spring (March–April): wheat, barley, gram (chana), mustard and peas.
Zaid crops are grown in the short summer season between rabi and kharif: watermelon, muskmelon, cucumber and some vegetables and fodder.
Soils differ: alluvial soil in the Northern Plains is very fertile; black soil (regur) of the Deccan holds moisture and is ideal for cotton; red soil gets its colour from iron.
Laterite soil forms in areas of high temperature and heavy rain and suits crops like cashew, tea and coffee; desert soil in Rajasthan is sandy and suits hardy crops like bajra.

ex.q: A farmer in Punjab grows rice from June to October and wheat from November to April. Which crop seasons is she using?
st: Rice is sown with the monsoon and harvested in autumn: that is kharif.
Wheat is sown in winter and harvested in spring: that is rabi.
Using both seasons lets her grow two crops a year on the same land.
ex.a: Rice is a kharif crop and wheat is a rabi crop.

topics.rl: Watermelons piled high on carts in May are zaid crops, grown in the short summer season.

topics.t: Water, farming practices and farmers' challenges
topics.h: A drip of water at the root of each plant can save far more water than flooding a whole field. Smart farming saves water!
p: Irrigation means supplying water to crops. Sources include canals, wells and tube-wells, tanks and ponds. Traditional systems include stepwells, johads in Rajasthan, kuhls in Himachal Pradesh and bamboo drip irrigation in Meghalaya.
Drip and sprinkler irrigation give water only where it is needed, saving a great deal of water.
Good practices: crop rotation (growing pulses after cereals helps restore soil fertility), mixed cropping, using compost and manure, and terrace farming on hill slopes to stop soil from washing away.
Many farmers face challenges: small landholdings, dependence on the monsoon, falling groundwater levels, soil damage from overuse of chemicals, and uncertain prices for crops.
The government supports farmers through Minimum Support Prices (MSP) for some crops, Soil Health Cards, crop insurance and farm loans through Kisan Credit Cards.

ex.q: A farmer grows rice and wheat on the same field year after year and the soil is getting weaker. What change could help?
st: Growing the same cereal crops again and again uses up the same nutrients.
Pulses such as moong or chana help restore nitrogen in the soil.
So rotating crops, by growing pulses in between, can make the soil healthier.
ex.a: Practise crop rotation, for example by growing pulses between cereal crops.

topics.rl: The step-like terraced fields you may see in pictures of Uttarakhand, Sikkim or Meghalaya are an example of farming adapted to hill slopes.

topics.h: If you walked along all of India's land borders, you would pass through deserts, plains, rivers, forests and the world's highest mountains!
p: India shares land borders with seven countries: Pakistan and Afghanistan in the north-west, China, Nepal and Bhutan in the north, and Bangladesh and Myanmar in the east.
India shares its longest land border with Bangladesh. Five Indian states touch Bangladesh: West Bengal, Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram.
Nepal borders Uttarakhand, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, West Bengal and Sikkim. Bhutan borders Sikkim, West Bengal, Assam and Arunachal Pradesh.
Myanmar borders four north-eastern states: Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Manipur and Mizoram.
Citizens of India, Nepal and Bhutan can travel across their borders without a visa, which shows the close ties among them.

ex.q: A student in Imphal, Manipur, wants to know which foreign country is closest to her home state. How can she work it out?
st: Manipur is in north-east India.
The countries bordering the north-east include China, Bhutan, Bangladesh and Myanmar.
Manipur's eastern border touches Myanmar.
ex.a: Myanmar, which borders Manipur.

topics.rl: Many families in border states like Sikkim, Bihar or West Bengal have relatives, festivals and foods in common with people across the border.

topics.h: Some of India's neighbours are across the sea. Sri Lanka is so close that it can be reached across a narrow strait!
p: Maritime neighbours are countries that are close to India across the sea. Sri Lanka and the Maldives are India's main maritime neighbours.
Sri Lanka lies to the south-east of India's southern tip. It is separated from Tamil Nadu by the narrow Palk Strait and the Gulf of Mannar.
The Maldives is a country of coral islands in the Indian Ocean, south of India's Lakshadweep islands. Its capital is Malé.
The Andaman and Nicobar Islands bring India close to Myanmar, Thailand and Indonesia across the sea. Indira Point in Great Nicobar is India's southernmost point.
The seas connect India with its maritime neighbours through fishing, trade, shipping and tourism, and they cooperate on ocean safety and disaster relief.

ex.q: Why can a boat from Rameswaram reach Sri Lanka much faster than one from Mumbai?
st: Rameswaram is on the Tamil Nadu coast, next to the Palk Strait.
The Palk Strait is a narrow strip of sea between India and Sri Lanka.
Mumbai is far away on the west coast.
ex.a: Because Rameswaram is right beside the narrow Palk Strait that separates India from Sri Lanka.

topics.rl: Many tourists from India visit the Maldives and Sri Lanka, and fishermen from both sides share the waters of the Palk Strait.

topics.h: The same poet, Rabindranath Tagore, wrote the national anthems of both India and Bangladesh!
p: India and her neighbours share a long history of trade, travel, languages, foods and faiths.
Buddhism links many neighbours: the Buddha was born at Lumbini in Nepal, Ashoka's son Mahinda took Buddhism to Sri Lanka, and Buddhism is a major faith in Bhutan, Sri Lanka and Myanmar.
Great rivers flow across borders: the Ganga continues into Bangladesh as the Padma, and the Brahmaputra flows from Tibet (where it is called the Yarlung Tsangpo) through India into Bangladesh.
Rabindranath Tagore wrote India's national anthem 'Jana Gana Mana' and Bangladesh's national anthem 'Amar Shonar Bangla'.
Neighbours cooperate through groups such as SAARC (set up in 1985 in Dhaka) and BIMSTEC, and by helping each other after disasters like earthquakes, floods and cyclones.

ex.q: Why do people in India and Nepal share many festivals, foods and temples?
st: Their lands touch along a long, open border.
People have travelled, traded and married across it for centuries.
So they share languages, faiths and customs, such as celebrating Dashain/Dussehra and visiting temples like Pashupatinath.
ex.a: Because centuries of travel, trade and family ties across an open border created a shared culture.

topics.rl: When you hear about Indian rescue teams helping a neighbour after an earthquake, you are seeing these ties in action.

topics.t: Harsha and the struggle for Kannauj
topics.h: For about two hundred years, three powerful dynasties fought again and again over one city: Kannauj!
p: After the Guptas declined, many regional kingdoms rose across India between the 6th and 10th centuries.
Harṣhavardhana (Harsha) ruled from 606 to 647 CE, first from Thanesar and then from Kannauj. His court poet Bāṇabhaṭṭa wrote his life story, the Harṣhacharita. Harsha himself wrote Sanskrit plays.
The Chinese pilgrim Xuanzang (Hiuen Tsang) visited India in Harsha's time and studied at Nālandā.
After Harsha, Kannauj on the Ganga became a prize city. The Gurjara-Pratīhāras, the Pālas and the Rāṣhṭrakūṭas fought for it; historians call this the Tripartite Struggle ('three-sided struggle').
The Pālas ruled Bengal and Bihar. Gopāla, the first Pāla king, is said to have been chosen by local chiefs. Dharmapāla founded the Buddhist university of Vikramashilā.

ex.q: Why did three distant dynasties all want to control Kannauj?
st: Kannauj stood on the Ganga in the fertile plains, with rich farmland and trade.
Since Harsha's time it was seen as the most important city of north India.
Controlling it brought wealth and great prestige.
ex.a: Because Kannauj was wealthy, on important routes, and a symbol of power in north India.

topics.rl: Kannauj in Uttar Pradesh is now famous for making attar (natural perfume), but it was once the capital that every empire wanted.

topics.h: In the 7th century, two southern kingdoms competed fiercely but also created some of India's most beautiful temples.
p: The Chālukyas of Bādāmi (Vātāpi) ruled much of the Deccan in present-day Karnataka. Their greatest king, Pulakeshin II, stopped Harsha's advance at the Narmada river.
Pulakeshin II's victories are recorded in the Aihole inscription, composed by his court poet Ravikīrti.
The Pallavas ruled from Kānchīpuram in present-day Tamil Nadu. Mahendravarman I was a king and a playwright. His son Narasiṁhavarman I, called Māmalla, captured Vātāpi in 642 CE.

The port town of Māmallapuram (Mahabalipuram) is named after Māmalla. It has the Pañcha Rathas (temples cut from single rocks), the great rock relief often called Arjuna's Penance, and the Shore Temple.
The Chālukyas built fine temples at Aihole, Bādāmi and Pattadakal. The temples at Pattadakal and the monuments at Mahabalipuram are UNESCO World Heritage Sites.

ex.q: Two kingdoms were rivals and fought many wars, yet both built magnificent temples. What does this tell us about the period?
st: Kings showed their power through victories and through grand buildings.
They supported architects, sculptors and poets.
So even in times of war, art and architecture flourished.
ex.a: That rulers competed not only in war but also in art and temple-building, so culture flourished.

topics.rl: The Shore Temple and the Pañcha Rathas at Mahabalipuram, near Chennai, attract visitors from all over the world.

topics.h: Imagine carving a whole temple, top to bottom, out of a single mountain of rock. The Rāṣhṭrakūṭas did it at Ellora!
p: The Rāṣhṭrakūṭas rose in the Deccan in the 8th century when Dantidurga overthrew the Chālukyas of Bādāmi. Their later capital was Mānyakheṭa.
King Kṛiṣhṇa I had the Kailāsa temple at Ellora carved from a single rock, from the top downwards. It is one of the largest rock-cut monuments in the world.
King Amoghavarṣha I supported literature; the Kavirājamārga, an early work on Kannada poetry, was written in his court.
In this period, the Ālvārs (devotees of Vishnu) and Nāyanārs (devotees of Shiva) composed devotional songs in Tamil, spreading bhakti, or loving devotion.
Great universities like Nālandā and Vikramashilā drew students from many lands. In 712 CE, Arab forces under Muhammad bin Qasim conquered Sindh, bringing new contacts with West Asia.

ex.q: Carving the Kailāsa temple began at the top of the rock and went downwards. Why might sculptors carve from the top?
st: When you remove rock from the top, it falls away without damaging the parts below.
Workers could stand on the uncut rock as a platform.
This avoided the need for tall scaffolding.
ex.a: Carving from the top let rock fall away safely and gave workers a place to stand, without scaffolding.

topics.rl: The Ellora caves near Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar (Aurangabad) have Buddhist, Hindu and Jain caves side by side: a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

topics.t: The Cholas: temples, navy and village assemblies
topics.h: A Tamil king built a temple so tall that its tower dominated the town of Thanjavur, and his son sent a navy across the sea to Southeast Asia!
p: The Chola dynasty rose again in the Kaveri delta when Vijayālaya captured Thanjavur in the 9th century.
Rājarāja I (985–1014 CE) built the great Bṛihadīshvara temple (Rājarājeshvaram) at Thanjavur, completed around 1010 CE.

His son Rājendra I (1014–1044 CE) led an army to the Ganga, took the title Gangaikoṇḍa Chola ('the Chola who brought the Ganga') and built a new capital, Gangaikoṇḍa Cholapuram. He also sent a naval expedition against Shrīvijaya in Southeast Asia.
Inscriptions at Uttaramerur (10th century) describe how members of village assemblies (sabhās) were chosen by drawing names written on palm-leaf tickets from a pot (kuḍavolai).
Chola artists made famous bronze images, such as Shiva as Naṭarāja, the Lord of Dance. The 'Great Living Chola Temples' are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

ex.q: The Uttaramerur inscriptions describe choosing assembly members by lot, with rules on who could stand. Why is this interesting for students of government?
st: Villages managed their own affairs through assemblies.
Members were chosen by a fixed, written procedure, not just by a ruler's order.
This shows an early form of local self-government with rules.
ex.a: It shows that Chola villages had organised local self-government with written rules for choosing members.

topics.rl: Many classical dancers pose like the Chola bronze Naṭarāja, and copies of it are found in museums around the world.

topics.h: In 1178, a queen of Gujarat led her army against an invader near Mount Abu and won!
p: In the 11th century, Mahmud of Ghazni (in present-day Afghanistan) raided north India many times, carrying away great wealth. Around 1025–26 he attacked the Somnath temple in Gujarat.
The scholar Al-Bīrūnī came to India in Mahmud's time, learned Sanskrit and wrote the Kitāb-ul-Hind, describing Indian sciences, beliefs and customs.
In the 12th century, Muhammad Ghori attacked. In 1178, Rānī Nāikī Devī of Gujarat, ruling for her young son, defeated him near Mount Abu.
In the First Battle of Tarain (1191), Prithvīrāj Chauhān defeated Ghori. In the Second Battle of Tarain (1192), Ghori won.
After Ghori's death, his general Quṭbuddīn Aibak began to rule from Delhi in 1206, starting the Delhi Sultanate. Many Indian rulers continued to resist in different regions.

ex.q: Prithvīrāj Chauhān won at Tarain in 1191 but lost in 1192. What does this show about history?
st: One battle's result is not the end of the story.
The defeated side may come back stronger after preparing better.
So historians study several events together to understand what changed.
ex.a: That outcomes can change quickly; history must be understood through a series of events, not one.

topics.rl: Tarain (Taraori) is in present-day Haryana, near Karnal, on the plains north of Delhi.

topics.t: New powers, thinkers and links with Southeast Asia
topics.h: While battles were fought in the north, poets, scholars and temple-builders across India were creating treasures that still shine today.
p: Many regional powers flourished: the Chandelas built the temples of Khajuraho, the Hoysaḷas built richly carved temples at Belur and Halebidu, and the Paramāra king Bhoja of Dhar was a famous scholar-king.
Thinkers and reformers: Rāmānujāchārya taught devotion to Vishnu; Basavaṇṇa in Karnataka wrote vachanas (sayings) in Kannada and taught that all people are equal before God.
Literature and science: Jayadeva wrote the Gīta Govinda; Kalhaṇa wrote the Rājataraṅgiṇī, a history of Kashmir; Bhāskarāchārya (Bhāskara II) wrote the mathematics book Līlāvatī.
India's links with Southeast Asia were strong. The Angkor Wat temple in Cambodia, dedicated to Vishnu, was built in the 12th century by King Sūryavarman II.
Despite invasions, Indian cultural practices, learning and temple traditions continued and adapted.

ex.q: Kalhaṇa's Rājataraṅgiṇī is a history of the kings of Kashmir written in the 12th century. Why is it special?
st: Most old Indian texts were poems, prayers or stories.
Kalhaṇa tried to record the history of kings in order and used older records.
So it is one of the earliest works in India written as a history.
ex.a: It is one of the earliest Indian texts that tries to record history in order, using older sources.

topics.rl: Belur and Halebidu in Karnataka, Khajuraho in Madhya Pradesh and Angkor Wat in Cambodia are all UNESCO World Heritage Sites.

topics.t: People who came and stayed: Jews and Christians
topics.h: In Kochi, there is a street called Jew Town, and nearby is a synagogue more than 450 years old. How did it get there?
p: Over thousands of years, many groups of people came to India as traders, travellers or people seeking safety. Many settled and became part of Indian society.

Jewish communities have lived in India for many centuries. The Cochin Jews lived in Kerala; the Paradesi Synagogue in Mattancherry, Kochi, was built in 1568. The Bene Israel lived along the Konkan coast of Maharashtra, and Baghdadi Jews settled later in Mumbai and Kolkata.
Jewish communities in India lived peacefully alongside their neighbours and kept their own traditions.

The Syriac (Saint Thomas) Christians of Kerala are among the oldest Christian communities in the world. According to their tradition, Saint Thomas, a disciple of Jesus, reached the Kerala coast in the 1st century CE.
These communities adopted local languages like Malayalam and Marathi, local dress and foods, while keeping their own faiths.

ex.q: The Cochin Jews spoke Malayalam, and Syriac Christians in Kerala wear local dress and cook Kerala food. What does this show?
st: Both groups kept their own faith and prayers.
At the same time, they adopted the language, food and dress of the land.
They became part of Kerala's society while keeping their identity.
ex.a: That communities can keep their own faith while sharing the local culture: they belong to India.

topics.rl: Kerala's port towns like Kochi and Kodungallur have synagogues, churches, mosques and temples close to one another.

topics.t: Parsis, Arab traders, Siddis and Armenians
topics.h: A story says that when Parsi refugees reached Gujarat, they promised to mix into society like sugar dissolves in milk, sweetening it without overflowing!
p: The Parsis are Zoroastrians who left Persia (Iran) and, according to their tradition (the Qissa-i-Sanjan), landed at Sanjan in Gujarat, where a local ruler let them settle. They keep their sacred fire burning in fire temples, such as the Iranshah at Udvada.
Parsis have contributed greatly to India: Dadabhai Naoroji, Jamsetji Tata and the scientist Homi J. Bhabha were Parsis.
Arab merchants traded along the Malabar coast for centuries. The Cheraman Juma Masjid at Kodungallur, Kerala, is believed to be one of the oldest mosques in India.

The Siddis are people of African descent who came across the Indian Ocean as sailors, traders and soldiers, and some were brought as slaves. They live in Gujarat, Karnataka and Maharashtra. Malik Ambar, of African origin, became a powerful minister of the Ahmadnagar kingdom.
Armenian traders settled in cities like Kolkata and Chennai. The Armenian Church of Holy Nazareth in Kolkata was built in 1724.

ex.q: In the story of the Parsis and the cup of milk, sugar is added to a full cup without making it overflow. What does this story mean?
st: The full cup of milk stands for the local land and people.
The sugar stands for the Parsi newcomers.
Sugar dissolves and sweetens milk without spilling it: newcomers can blend in and enrich society.
ex.a: That the newcomers would blend in peacefully and make society richer, like sugar in milk.

topics.rl: Parsi New Year (Navroz), Christmas, Id, Diwali and many other festivals are celebrated in India, and friends often share sweets across communities.

topics.t: India's pluralism: a home to many
topics.h: The ancient phrase 'Vasudhaiva Kuṭumbakam' means 'the world is one family'. India has tried to live this idea for centuries.
p: Pluralism means many communities, faiths, languages and customs living together with respect, each keeping its identity.
India is the birthplace of Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism and Sikhism, and it is also home to Muslims, Christians, Parsis, Jews and many other communities.
India has also given shelter to refugees. In 1959, the Dalai Lama and many Tibetans came to India; Tibetan settlements grew in places like Dharamshala (Himachal Pradesh) and Bylakuppe (Karnataka).
The Constitution protects this pluralism: it gives freedom of religion to all and treats all citizens equally.
Pluralism grows through everyday acts: sharing festivals and food, learning each other's languages and respecting different beliefs.

ex.q: Aman, Mary, Gurpreet and Tenzin are classmates. They celebrate Id, Christmas, Gurpurab and Losar, and share sweets with each other. What value do they show?
st: Each child keeps their own festival and tradition.
They also respect and enjoy each other's festivals.
Living together with respect while keeping one's identity is pluralism.
ex.a: Pluralism: respect for many faiths and cultures living together.

topics.rl: In many Indian cities you can hear temple bells, the azaan, church bells and gurbani within the same neighbourhood.

topics.ch: The State, the Government, and You
topics.h: Governments come and go after elections, but India stays India. That's because the State and the government are not the same thing!
p: A State (country) has four elements: a defined territory, a population, a government and sovereignty (the power to make its own decisions without outside control).
The government is the group of people and institutions that run the State: they make laws, carry them out and settle disputes.
Governments change, for example after elections, but the State continues. India the State has existed since independence while many different governments have come and gone.
India is a democracy, because citizens elect their representatives, and a republic, because its head of state, the President, is elected and does not inherit the post.
In everyday speech, 'state' can also mean a part of India, like Kerala or Punjab. In this chapter, 'State' with a capital S means the whole country.

ex.q: After a general election, a new party forms the government in New Delhi. Has the Indian State changed?
st: The territory, the people and India's sovereignty are the same.
Only the people running the government have changed.
The government is one part of the State; it can change while the State continues.
ex.a: No. The government has changed, but the State of India continues.

topics.rl: Your school stays the same even when a new principal takes charge, just as the State stays the same when a new government takes office.

topics.ch: The State, the Government, and You
topics.t: Three organs and three tiers of government
topics.h: One group makes the rules, another carries them out, and a third settles arguments about them. That's how power is shared!
p: The government has three organs. The legislature makes laws; the executive carries out (implements) laws; the judiciary interprets laws and settles disputes.

At the national level, Parliament (the President, the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha) is the legislature. The Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers lead the executive. The Supreme Court, in New Delhi, is the highest court.
Keeping these organs separate, so that each checks the others, is called separation of powers. The judiciary in India is independent.
India has three tiers (levels) of government: the Union (central) government, State governments and local governments.

Local governments include panchayats in villages (gram panchayat, panchayat samiti and zila parishad) and municipalities and municipal corporations in towns and cities. The 73rd and 74th Amendments (1992) gave them constitutional status.

ex.q: A street light near your home is broken. Which tier of government should you ask to repair it?
st: Street lights are a local matter.
In a town or city, the municipality or municipal corporation handles them; in a village, the gram panchayat.
So the local tier is the right level.
ex.a: The local government: the municipality, municipal corporation or gram panchayat.

topics.rl: Your gram panchayat or municipal ward member, your MLA and your MP represent you at the three levels of government.

topics.ch: The State, the Government, and You
topics.t: You and the government: a citizen's role
topics.h: Democracy is not just about voting once in five years. Citizens can question, suggest, complain and help, every day!
p: Citizens take part in government by voting in elections at all three tiers, from panchayat to Parliament, once they are 18.
In villages, every adult voter is a member of the gram sabha and can discuss village plans and question the panchayat.
The Right to Information Act, 2005, lets citizens ask government offices for information about their work.
Citizens can approach courts if their rights are violated, and they pay taxes that fund schools, roads and hospitals.
Good citizens also follow laws, protect public property, keep their surroundings clean and respect the rights of others. Children can start by being informed and responsible.

ex.q: A road in a village was supposed to be repaired, but nothing has happened. Name two ways villagers could act.
st: They can raise the issue at the gram sabha meeting and ask the panchayat for answers.
They can use the Right to Information Act to ask how the money for the road was spent.
They can also contact their elected representatives.
ex.a: Raise it in the gram sabha and use the RTI Act (or contact their representatives).

topics.rl: When your school holds a student council election or a cleanliness drive, you are practising the habits of an active citizen.

topics.h: Your morning milk, the bus to school, the light in your classroom and the water in the tap all depend on something invisible: infrastructure!
p: Infrastructure means the basic facilities and services a country needs to work and grow, like roads, railways, ports, airports, electricity, water supply, telephones and the internet.
Physical infrastructure includes transport, energy, water and communication networks. Social infrastructure includes schools, hospitals and other services for people.
Good infrastructure helps farmers sell crops, factories get raw materials, children reach school and patients reach hospitals. That is why it is called an engine of development.

Many infrastructure facilities are public goods: once provided, they can be used by everyone, and one person's use does not stop another's. Street lights, lighthouses and national defence are examples.
Because private companies may not earn profits from public goods, governments usually build and pay for them using tax money.

ex.q: A village gets a new all-weather road to the town. List two ways this can change villagers' lives.
st: Farmers can take vegetables and milk to the town market quickly and get better prices.
Children can reach a school and patients can reach a hospital even in the rainy season.
Buses and shops may come to the village, creating jobs.
ex.a: Any two: better prices for farm goods, easier access to schools and hospitals, more transport and jobs.

topics.rl: A street light outside your home lights the road for everyone who walks by; that's a public good in action.

topics.h: On 16 April 1853, India's first passenger train puffed 34 km from Bori Bunder in Mumbai to Thane. Today trains carry crores of passengers!
p: India has one of the largest road networks in the world: National Highways, State Highways, district roads and village roads. The Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (2000) connects villages with all-weather roads.
