The Golden Quadrilateral highway links Delhi, Mumbai, Chennai and Kolkata. The North–South corridor links Srinagar and Kanyakumari, and the East–West corridor links Silchar and Porbandar.

Indian Railways' first passenger train ran on 16 April 1853 between Bori Bunder (Mumbai) and Thane. The Chenab Bridge in Jammu and Kashmir is the world's highest railway arch bridge. India's first metro railway opened in Kolkata in 1984.
Air transport is the fastest way to travel long distances. The UDAN scheme aims to make flights affordable and connect smaller towns.
Most of India's foreign trade by volume travels by sea through ports like Mumbai, Jawaharlal Nehru Port (Navi Mumbai), Chennai, Kolkata, Visakhapatnam, Kochi and Paradip.

ex.q: A train leaves Bori Bunder and travels the same 34 km route to Thane as the first train. If it covers 17 km in the first half hour at the same speed, how long will the whole trip take?
st: Half an hour covers 17 km.
34 km is 2 × 17 km.
So it takes 2 × half an hour = 1 hour.
ex.a: 1 hour

topics.rl: When your family books a train or flight on an app, or orders something shipped from another city, you are using India's transport infrastructure.

topics.t: Power, communication and our shared responsibility
topics.h: A tiny phone in a village can now make a video call to a doctor in a big city. Power lines and internet cables make it possible!
p: Electricity comes from many sources: thermal power (from coal or gas), hydroelectric power (from flowing water), nuclear power, and renewable sources like solar and wind energy.
Renewable energy, especially solar and wind, is growing quickly in India because it does not run out and causes less pollution. Rajasthan and Gujarat have large solar parks.

Communication infrastructure includes India Post, telephones, mobile networks and the internet. The six-digit PIN code system was introduced in 1972. BharatNet aims to bring broadband internet to every gram panchayat.
Good internet lets people use online banking, learning, health services and government services from home.
Infrastructure is a shared responsibility. Citizens should not damage public property, waste electricity or water, or litter on roads and trains, because repairs cost public money.

ex.q: A family switches off fans and lights when leaving a room. How does this small act help the whole country?
st: Less electricity is wasted.
Less coal needs to be burnt in thermal plants, so there is less pollution.
More power is available for homes, hospitals and factories.
ex.a: It saves electricity, reduces pollution and leaves more power for others.

topics.rl: Look at your electricity bill or a solar panel on a rooftop; these show how energy infrastructure reaches your home.

topics.ch: Banks and the Magic of Finance
topics.h: When you put ₹100 in a bank, it doesn't just sit in a box with your name on it. The bank puts it to work!
p: A bank accepts deposits (money people keep with it) and gives loans (money lent to people and businesses).
Banks pay interest to depositors and charge a higher rate of interest on loans. The difference helps the bank pay its costs and earn a profit.
Banks also keep money and valuables safe, help people make payments, and offer services like lockers, cheques, cards and online banking.

The Reserve Bank of India (RBI), with its headquarters in Mumbai, is India's central bank. It issues currency notes, acts as the bank for the government and for other banks (the 'banker's bank'), and makes rules for banks.
Banks link savers and borrowers: the savings of many people become loans for farmers, students, shopkeepers and businesses, helping the economy grow.

ex.q: A bank pays 4% interest a year on deposits and charges 9% a year on loans. If it lends ₹100 from deposits for a year, how much more does it earn than it pays?
st: Interest earned on the loan: 9% of ₹100 = ₹9.
Interest paid to the depositor: 4% of ₹100 = ₹4.
Difference = ₹9 − ₹4 = ₹5.

topics.rl: When your parents take an education loan or a home loan, the money comes from the savings of many depositors.

topics.ch: Banks and the Magic of Finance
topics.h: A savings account, a fixed deposit and a recurring deposit are like three kinds of piggy banks, each with its own rules.
p: A savings account is for individuals to keep money safely and earn some interest; money can be withdrawn when needed.
A current account is mainly for businesses that make many payments every day; it usually pays little or no interest.
A fixed deposit (FD) keeps a lump sum for a fixed period at a higher interest rate. A recurring deposit (RD) lets you deposit a fixed amount every month for a fixed period.
People borrow from banks for homes, education, farming and business. Borrowers must repay the loan with interest, so they should borrow only what they can repay.
Through the Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana (2014), crores of people opened zero-balance bank accounts, bringing many families into the banking system.

ex.q: Meera puts ₹500 in a recurring deposit every month for 12 months. How much has she deposited in total (before interest)?
st: Monthly deposit: ₹500.
Number of months: 12.

topics.rl: Many schools encourage children to open a savings account with a parent, so they learn early to save regularly.

topics.ch: Banks and the Magic of Finance
topics.t: Interest and the magic of compounding
topics.h: Keep ₹1,000 in a bank at 10% and leave it alone. In the second year, you earn interest even on your interest. That's the magic of compounding!
p: Interest is the extra money paid for using someone else's money. The money deposited or borrowed is called the principal.
Simple interest is calculated only on the principal: Simple Interest = Principal × Rate × Time ÷ 100.
Compound interest is calculated on the principal plus the interest already added. So the amount grows faster each year.
With compounding, money grows faster the longer it stays invested. That's why starting to save early helps a lot.
Compounding works against borrowers too: unpaid loans, especially on credit cards, can grow very quickly.

ex.q: Find the simple interest and the compound interest on ₹1,000 at 10% a year for 2 years.
st: Simple interest: 1,000 × 10 × 2 ÷ 100 = ₹200.
Compound: after year 1, 1,000 + 100 = ₹1,100.
Year 2 interest = 10% of 1,100 = ₹110, so the amount is ₹1,210.
Compound interest = 1,210 − 1,000 = ₹210.
ex.a: Simple interest ₹200; compound interest ₹210.

topics.rl: Your grandparents may say 'save a little every month'. Because of compounding, small savings started early can grow large over many years.

topics.ch: Banks and the Magic of Finance
topics.t: Payments, the stock market and staying safe
topics.h: Banks will NEVER ask for your PIN or OTP on a call. If someone does, it's a trick!
p: Payments can be made by cash, cheque, demand draft, debit or credit card, net banking (NEFT, RTGS, IMPS) and UPI on a phone.

A share is a small part of the ownership of a company. Shares are bought and sold on stock exchanges such as the Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE, started in 1875, Asia's oldest stock exchange) and the National Stock Exchange (NSE).
Share prices go up and down, so investing in shares has risk. The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI) regulates the stock market to protect investors.
Common frauds include fake calls, messages or links asking for your PIN, OTP, CVV or passwords, and offers that promise unbelievable returns.
Stay safe: never share your PIN, OTP or passwords; do not click unknown links; check before you pay; and report cyber fraud quickly on the national helpline 1930.

ex.q: Kabir gets a call: 'I'm from your bank. Your account will be blocked. Tell me the OTP you just received.' What should he do?
st: Banks never ask for an OTP or PIN over a call.
Sharing the OTP would let the caller take money from the account.
So he should refuse, cut the call, tell an adult and report it to the bank or the 1930 helpline.
ex.a: Refuse, hang up, tell an adult and report the call.

topics.rl: Watch for the posters at banks and ATMs that warn 'Never share your PIN or OTP'; they are there for everyone's safety.

qa.q: Which physical region of India lies to the far north?
qa.e: The Himalayan mountains form India's northern boundary like a great wall.

qa.q: The Thar Desert is found mainly in which state?
qa.e: The Thar, or Great Indian Desert, covers much of western Rajasthan.

qa.q: Which hills in Rajasthan are among the oldest fold mountains in the world?
qa.e: The Aravallis are extremely old and have been worn down over a very long time.

qa.q: Why are the Northern Plains so good for farming?
qa.a: Rivers have spread fertile soil over flat land
qa.e: Rivers from the Himalayas deposit fine fertile soil (alluvium), and the land is flat with plenty of water.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT one of India's physical regions?
qa.e: The Sahara is in Africa. India's desert is the Thar.

qa.q: How does India's variety of landforms affect people's lives?
qa.a: It shapes their food, homes, clothes and work
qa.e: People adapt to their land: flat plains suit farming, mountains suit herding, coasts suit fishing.

qa.q: A region of high flat land, raised above the land around it, is called a:
qa.e: A plateau is a raised, fairly flat area, like a table-top. The Deccan Plateau is an example.

qa.q: Which island group of India lies in the Arabian Sea?
qa.e: Lakshadweep lies off the coast of Kerala in the Arabian Sea.

qa.q: What does the word 'Himalaya' mean?
qa.e: In Sanskrit, 'hima' means snow and 'alaya' means home or abode.

qa.q: Kangchenjunga, one of the world's highest peaks, lies on the border of Sikkim and which country?
qa.e: Kangchenjunga stands on the border between Sikkim (India) and Nepal, in the Greater Himalayas.

qa.q: Which is the outermost and lowest range of the Himalayas?
qa.e: The Shiwaliks are the southernmost, lowest range, next to the plains.

qa.q: The Himalayas are called 'young fold mountains' because:
qa.a: They were formed recently in Earth's history and are still rising
qa.e: In Earth's long history, the Himalayas formed fairly recently by the folding of rock layers, and they are still slowly rising.

qa.q: Why do Himalayan rivers flow throughout the year?
qa.a: They are fed by melting snow and glaciers
qa.e: Snow and glacier melt keeps them flowing even in dry months, so they are perennial.

qa.q: How were the Northern Plains formed?
qa.a: By soil deposited by rivers over a very long time
qa.e: The Indus, Ganga and Brahmaputra and their tributaries carried silt down from the mountains and spread it over the plains.

qa.q: Which river system flows through Assam in the north-east?
qa.e: The Brahmaputra flows through Assam, forming a broad valley.

qa.q: Majuli, one of the world's largest river islands, is found in which river?
qa.e: Majuli is a large river island in the Brahmaputra in Assam.

qa.q: Which mountain range is also called the Sahyadri?
qa.e: The Western Ghats along the west coast are also known as the Sahyadri.

qa.q: How are the Eastern Ghats different from the Western Ghats?
qa.a: They are lower and broken up by rivers
qa.e: The Eastern Ghats are lower and are cut through by big rivers flowing to the Bay of Bengal.

qa.q: Which river of the plateau flows into the Bay of Bengal?
qa.e: The Godavari flows east to the Bay of Bengal. The Narmada and Tapi flow west into the Arabian Sea.

qa.q: Lakshadweep islands are made mainly of:
qa.e: Lakshadweep's islands are coral islands built over a long time by tiny sea creatures.

qa.q: Where is India's only active volcano?
qa.a: Barren Island in the Andaman Sea
qa.e: Barren Island, part of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands, has India's only active volcano.

qa.q: Which coastal plain of India is wider and has large river deltas?
qa.e: The east coast is wider because big rivers deposit soil there and form deltas.

qa.q: The Sundarbans, famous for mangroves and the Royal Bengal tiger, lie in the delta of:
qa.e: The Sundarbans are on the vast delta formed where the Ganga and Brahmaputra meet the Bay of Bengal.

qa.q: Why are the rocks of the Peninsular Plateau special?
qa.a: They are among the oldest rocks in India
qa.e: The plateau is built of ancient hard rocks, much older than the Himalayas.

qa.q: Weather means the condition of the atmosphere:
qa.a: At a place over a short time
qa.e: Weather is about the air at a place now or over a few hours or days. The long-term average is climate.

qa.q: The amount of water vapour in the air is called:
qa.e: Humidity measures moisture in the air. High humidity makes us feel sticky.

qa.q: Wind blows from:
qa.a: High pressure areas to low pressure areas
qa.e: Air moves from where pressure is higher to where it is lower, just like air rushing out of a pumped-up balloon.

qa.q: What happens to air pressure as you climb a high mountain?
qa.e: There is less air above you at greater heights, so the air pressure is lower.

qa.q: Which of these is a form of precipitation?
qa.e: Precipitation is water falling from clouds: rain, snow, sleet or hail. Dew and fog form near the ground and do not fall from clouds.

qa.q: On a very humid day, why do we feel sticky?
qa.e: When the air is full of moisture, sweat evaporates slowly, so it stays on our skin.

qa.q: Which pair are both elements of weather?
qa.e: Temperature and wind describe the state of the air. The others are features of the land.

qa.q: Which statement describes weather, not climate?
qa.a: It is raining heavily in Kolkata this evening
qa.e: 'This evening' is a short time at one place: that is weather. The others are long-term patterns, which is climate.

qa.q: Which instrument measures air pressure?
qa.e: A barometer measures the pressure of the air.

qa.q: An anemometer is used to measure:
qa.e: The anemometer's cups spin faster in stronger wind, measuring speed. Direction is shown by a wind vane.

qa.q: Rainfall is usually measured in:
qa.e: A rain gauge shows the depth of rain collected, measured in millimetres.

qa.q: Why are thermometers at a weather station kept inside a shaded, airy box?
qa.a: So direct sunlight does not heat them and give a wrong reading
qa.e: We want the temperature of the air, not of a thermometer heated by sunshine, so it is kept in the shade with air flowing through.

qa.q: A town's highest temperature today was 36 °C and the lowest was 24 °C. What was the difference in °C?
qa.e: Difference = 36 − 24 = 12 °C.

qa.q: A school recorded rain: Mon 8 mm, Tue 20 mm, Wed 0 mm, Thu 12 mm. What was the total?
Which organisation gives official weather forecasts for India?
qa.e: The IMD is India's national weather service and issues forecasts and warnings.

qa.q: A hygrometer tells you:
qa.a: How much moisture is in the air
qa.e: A hygrometer measures humidity, the water vapour in the air.

qa.q: What is a weather forecast?
qa.a: A scientific prediction of coming weather
qa.e: Forecasts use measurements and science to predict what the weather is likely to be.

qa.q: Which tool lets forecasters watch a cyclone forming far out at sea?
qa.e: Satellites in space photograph clouds and storms over the ocean.

qa.q: Climate is best described as:
qa.a: The average weather of a place over many years
qa.e: Climate is the long-term pattern, usually averaged over 30 years or more.

qa.q: Why is an early cyclone warning useful for coastal villages?
qa.a: People get time to move to safe places and secure boats
qa.e: A warning cannot stop a cyclone, but it gives time to prepare and stay safe.

qa.q: A farmer hears that rain is expected in two days. How can this help her?
qa.a: She can plan sowing so seeds get the rainwater
qa.e: Sowing just before rain helps seeds get water naturally.

qa.q: Which of these people most needs a wind and sea forecast before work?
qa.a: A fisherman going out to sea
qa.e: Strong winds and rough seas are dangerous for small fishing boats.

qa.q: In which year was the India Meteorological Department set up?
qa.e: The IMD was established in 1875.

qa.q: Which statement is about climate?
qa.a: Mawsynram gets very heavy rain year after year
qa.e: A pattern repeated year after year is climate. The others describe a single time.

qa.q: Climate means:
qa.a: The average weather of a place over a long period
qa.e: Climate is the long-term average, usually over 30 years or more.

qa.q: Why is Ooty cool in summer while the plains below are hot?
qa.a: It is at a high altitude
qa.e: Temperature falls as height increases, so hill towns are cooler.

qa.q: Which line of latitude passes through the middle of India?
qa.e: The Tropic of Cancer (about 23½° N) crosses India from Gujarat to Mizoram.

qa.q: Why does Mumbai have a moderate climate?
qa.a: It is next to the sea
qa.e: The sea warms and cools slowly, keeping coastal temperatures mild.

qa.q: How do the Himalayas affect India's climate?
qa.a: They block very cold winds from Central Asia
qa.e: The high wall of mountains shields the plains from icy northern winds and also traps monsoon winds.

qa.q: Which city is likely to have the biggest difference between summer and winter temperatures?
qa.e: Delhi is far from the sea, so it has very hot summers and cold winters. The others are coastal.

qa.q: Places near the Equator are generally:
qa.e: The Sun's rays fall more directly near the Equator, so these places are warmer.

qa.q: The western side of the Western Ghats gets heavy rain, while the eastern side gets much less. The drier eastern side is called a:
qa.e: Moist winds rise and drop rain on the windward (west) side; by the time they cross the Ghats they are dry, leaving a rain-shadow area.

qa.q: The word 'monsoon' comes from 'mausim', which means:
qa.e: Mausim means season; monsoon winds change direction with the seasons.

qa.q: The south-west monsoon usually reaches which state first?
qa.e: Kerala, at the south-western tip, receives the monsoon first, usually around 1 June.

qa.q: Why do the summer monsoon winds blow from the sea towards the land?
qa.a: The land becomes much hotter than the sea, creating low pressure over land
qa.e: Hot land creates low pressure; moist air from the higher-pressure sea moves in.

qa.q: Which months make up the south-west monsoon season?
qa.e: The south-west monsoon season runs from June to September.

qa.q: Which part of India receives a lot of rain from the north-east (winter) monsoon?
qa.e: Winter winds pick up moisture over the Bay of Bengal and drop rain on the Tamil Nadu coast.

qa.q: Which of these is a traditional Indian ṛitu for the rainy season?
qa.e: Varṣhā is the season of rains. Vasanta is spring, Grīṣhma summer and Shishira winter.

qa.q: How many traditional ṛitus are there in the Indian calendar?
qa.e: The traditional calendar has six ṛitus of about two months each.

qa.q: What can happen when the monsoon is weak or late?
qa.a: Crops may suffer from lack of water
qa.e: Many farms depend on monsoon rain, so a weak monsoon can reduce harvests.

qa.q: Which of these is a cold desert?
qa.e: Ladakh is very cold and gets very little precipitation, so it is called a cold desert.

qa.q: Mawsynram and Sohra (Cherrapunji), among the wettest places on Earth, are in:
qa.e: Both are on the southern slopes of the Khasi Hills in Meghalaya.

qa.q: What is the 'loo'?
qa.a: A hot, dry wind in the northern plains in summer
qa.e: The loo blows across north India in May and June and can cause heatstroke.

qa.q: Which region gets the least rainfall?
qa.e: Western Rajasthan, in the Thar Desert, is one of the driest parts of India.

qa.q: Why do people in hot deserts often wear loose, light-coloured cotton clothes?
qa.e: Light colours reflect sunlight and loose cotton lets air flow over the skin.

qa.q: Steeply sloping roofs are most useful in places with:
qa.e: Slopes help rainwater drain away quickly.

qa.q: Which pair is correctly matched?
qa.e: Kerala gets heavy rain and stays warm. The other pairs are mismatched.

qa.q: Why do people in Ladakh keep animals like yaks and goats?
qa.a: These animals survive the cold and give milk, wool and transport
qa.e: In the cold, dry mountains, herding hardy animals is a good way to earn a living.

qa.q: What does 'janapada' mean?
qa.a: The land where a people set foot and settled
qa.e: Jana means people; pada means foot. A janapada was a territory settled by a people.

qa.q: Which is the oldest of the four Vedas?
qa.e: The Rigveda is the earliest Vedic text.

qa.q: How many Vedas are there?
qa.e: There are four Vedas: Rig, Sama, Yajur and Atharva.

qa.q: What were the sabhā and the samiti?
qa.e: Vedic texts mention these gatherings where people discussed important matters.

qa.q: A 'jana' was:
qa.e: A jana was a group of people, a clan or tribe.

qa.q: After the decline of the Harappan cities, people in northern India lived mostly in:
qa.e: For many centuries, life was mainly village-based before new cities rose again.

qa.q: How did some janapadas become mahājanapadas?
qa.a: By growing in land, people and wealth
qa.e: Stronger janapadas expanded and became 'great janapadas'.

qa.q: Why are the Vedas useful to historians?
qa.a: They tell us about the life and beliefs of the people who composed them
qa.e: The Vedas are a window into the ideas, prayers and society of their time.

qa.q: How many mahājanapadas are named in the old Buddhist and Jain lists?
qa.e: The texts list sixteen great janapadas.

qa.q: What was the capital of Magadha before Pāṭaliputra?
qa.e: Rājagṛiha (modern Rajgir in Bihar) was Magadha's early capital.

qa.q: Vaishālī was the capital of which mahājanapada?
qa.e: Vaishālī was the centre of the Vajji, a well-known gaṇa or saṅgha.

qa.q: In a gaṇa or saṅgha, power was held by:
qa.a: A group, with decisions discussed in assemblies
qa.e: Gaṇas were ruled collectively; many leaders met in assemblies.

qa.q: Ujjayinī was the capital of:
qa.e: Ujjayinī, today's Ujjain in Madhya Pradesh, was the capital of Avanti.

qa.q: Why did mahājanapadas collect taxes?
qa.a: To pay for armies, officials and walls
qa.e: Kings and councils needed wealth to keep armies, build forts and pay officials.

qa.q: Which mahājanapada finally became the most powerful?
qa.e: Magadha, in present-day Bihar, grew strongest and later became the centre of empires.

qa.q: Takshashilā, a famous centre of learning, was the capital of:
qa.e: Takshashilā was in Gandhāra in the north-west.

qa.q: The rise of cities in the Ganga plains from about the 6th century BCE is often called:
qa.e: The Harappan cities were India's first cities; the Ganga-plain cities came much later, so this is the second urbanisation.

qa.q: Which metal's use helped clear forests and grow more food?
qa.e: Iron axes and ploughs made clearing and farming easier.

qa.q: What were punch-marked coins mostly made of?
qa.e: Early Indian punch-marked coins were mostly silver pieces stamped with symbols.

qa.q: Why did many early cities build walls and moats?
qa.e: Fortifications defended the city's wealth and people from enemies.

qa.q: A shreṇī was:
qa.a: A guild of craftspeople or traders
qa.e: Shreṇīs were associations of people in the same craft or trade.

qa.q: Northern Black Polished Ware is a kind of:
qa.e: This glossy black pottery is found at many sites of this period.

qa.q: Which great teachers lived in the age of the early cities and mahājanapadas?
qa.e: The Buddha and Mahāvīra lived around the 6th–5th centuries BCE.

qa.q: Why could cities support people who did not farm?
qa.a: Farmers grew extra food that could be traded
qa.e: Surplus food from villages fed traders, crafts workers and officials in towns.

qa.q: Magadha was located mainly in present-day:
qa.e: Magadha lay in the middle Ganga plains, in today's Bihar.

qa.q: Which natural resource near Magadha helped it make strong weapons?
qa.e: Iron ore deposits allowed Magadha to make tools and weapons.

qa.q: Why were Magadha's forests important for its army?
qa.e: Elephants from the forests were a powerful part of Magadha's army.

qa.q: What was Magadha's early capital, surrounded by hills?
qa.e: Rājagṛiha (Rajgir) was surrounded by hills, which gave natural protection.

qa.q: Pāṭaliputra, Magadha's later capital, is the modern city of:
qa.e: Pāṭaliputra grew on the Ganga at the site of present-day Patna.

qa.q: Which dynasty ruled Magadha just before the Mauryas?
qa.e: Chandragupta Maurya overthrew the last Nanda king.

qa.q: Bimbisāra and Ajātashatru belonged to which dynasty?
qa.e: They were early Haryanka rulers who expanded Magadha.

qa.q: How did fertile land make Magadha stronger?
qa.a: More crops meant more food and more taxes for the ruler
qa.e: Surplus crops fed the people and the army, and taxes on them filled the treasury.

qa.q: Who founded the Mauryan Empire?
qa.e: Chandragupta Maurya founded it around 321 BCE.

qa.q: Who was Chandragupta's teacher and adviser?
qa.e: Chāṇakya, also known as Kauṭilya, guided Chandragupta.

qa.q: The Arthashāstra is a book about:
qa.e: It discusses statecraft: government, taxes, army, trade and law.

qa.q: How many 'limbs' of the state does the saptāṅga idea describe?
qa.e: 'Sapta' means seven: king, ministers, territory with people, fort, treasury, army and allies.

qa.q: Megasthenes was:
qa.a: A Greek ambassador at Chandragupta's court
qa.e: Seleucus sent him to Pāṭaliputra, and he wrote Indica.

qa.q: What was the capital of the Mauryan Empire?
qa.e: Pāṭaliputra (Patna) was the Mauryan capital.

qa.q: Which is the correct order of Mauryan rulers?
qa.e: Chandragupta was followed by his son Bindusāra and then his grandson Ashoka.

qa.q: Why is the Arthashāstra's list of 'allies' important for a kingdom?
qa.a: Friendly kingdoms can help in times of war and trade
qa.e: Good relations with other states make a kingdom safer and stronger.

qa.q: Which war changed Ashoka's heart?
qa.e: The suffering caused by the Kalinga war made Ashoka give up conquest by war.

qa.q: Ancient Kalinga lay mostly in present-day:
qa.e: Kalinga covered much of today's Odisha on the east coast.

qa.q: Which script were most of Ashoka's edicts written in?
qa.e: Most edicts use Brāhmī, an ancient script from which many Indian scripts later developed.

qa.q: Who deciphered the Brāhmī script in 1837?
qa.e: James Prinsep, working in Kolkata, cracked the script in 1837.

qa.q: How many spokes does the Ashoka Chakra on the national flag have?
qa.e: The Ashoka Chakra has 24 spokes.

qa.q: Which of these was part of Ashoka's dhamma?
qa.a: Kindness to animals and respect for all faiths
qa.e: Dhamma stressed kindness, truth, respect for elders and tolerance.

qa.q: India's National Emblem is taken from Ashoka's pillar at:
qa.e: The Lion Capital found at Sarnath near Varanasi was adopted as the emblem.

qa.q: Which of Ashoka's children is linked with taking Buddhism to Sri Lanka?
qa.e: Ashoka's son Mahinda went to Sri Lanka with the Buddha's teachings.

qa.q: Who founded the Shunga dynasty?
qa.e: Pushyamitra, a Mauryan general, overthrew Bṛihadratha around 185 BCE.

qa.q: The Sātavāhanas ruled mainly in:
qa.e: Their kingdom was in the Deccan, with Pratiṣhṭhāna on the Godavari as a capital.

qa.q: What is unusual about names like Gautamīputra Sātakarṇi?
qa.a: The king is named after his mother
qa.e: Gautamīputra means 'son of Gautamī', his mother.

qa.q: Khāravela's deeds are recorded in the:
qa.e: The Hāthīgumphā inscription is in the Udayagiri hills near Bhubaneswar.

qa.q: Which faith did Khāravela follow?
qa.e: Khāravela was a follower of Jainism and supported Jain monks.

qa.q: Which three kingdoms ruled Tamilakam in this period?
qa.e: The 'three crowned kings' of the Tamil region were the Cheras, Cholas and Pāṇḍyas.

qa.q: Sangam literature is written in:
qa.e: Sangam poems are among the oldest works of Tamil literature.

qa.q: Why is this period called an 'age of reorganisation'?
qa.a: Power was shared among many new kingdoms after the Mauryan Empire
qa.e: After the Mauryas, many kingdoms rose in different regions while trade and culture went on.

qa.q: Which Indo-Greek king is remembered in the Milinda-pañha?
qa.e: Menander, called Milinda in Indian texts, asks the monk Nāgasena about Buddhism.

qa.q: The monk who answered Milinda's questions was:
qa.e: Nāgasena is the Buddhist monk in the Milinda-pañha.

qa.q: Heliodorus set up his pillar in honour of:
qa.e: The Besnagar pillar honours Vāsudeva, showing a Greek adopting an Indian faith.

qa.q: Rudradāman was a ruler of the:
qa.e: Rudradāman was a famous Shaka ruler in western India.

qa.q: Rudradāman's Junagadh inscription records the repair of:
qa.e: It describes how the Sudarshana lake, a reservoir, was repaired.

qa.q: Who was the greatest Kushāna ruler?
qa.e: Kanishka ruled a large Kushāna kingdom and supported Buddhism.

qa.q: Puruṣhapura, a Kushāna capital, is today's:
qa.e: Puruṣhapura is modern Peshawar.

qa.q: What does the story of the newcomers show about Indian society at this time?
qa.a: Many outsiders adopted Indian ways and became part of it
qa.e: Greeks, Shakas and Kushānas took Indian names, languages and faiths.

qa.q: Which spice from India was so valued that it was called 'black gold'?
qa.e: Black pepper from the Malabar coast was in huge demand in the Roman world.

qa.q: The Silk Route linked:
qa.a: China, Central Asia, India and the Mediterranean
qa.e: The Silk Route was a network of land routes across Asia to the Mediterranean.

qa.q: Why have Roman coins been found in south India?
qa.a: Romans paid for Indian goods like spices and cloth
qa.e: The coins show active trade between south India and the Roman world.

qa.q: Which ancient trading site is near Puducherry?
qa.e: Arikamedu was an ancient port-town where Roman pottery has been found.

qa.q: How did ancient sailors use the monsoon?
qa.a: Seasonal winds helped them sail across the sea
qa.e: Knowing when the winds changed direction let ships sail to and from India.

qa.q: Gandhāra art is known for:
qa.e: Gandhāra sculptors mixed Greek styles with Buddhist themes.

qa.q: Mathurā sculptures were mostly made of:
qa.e: The Mathurā school used the local red sandstone.

qa.q: The carved gateways at the Great Stupa of Sanchi are called:
qa.e: Toraṇas are the decorated gateways around the stupa.

qa.q: Around which year did Chandragupta I make the Gupta kingdom strong?
qa.e: The Gupta rise is dated to around 320 CE, in the 4th century CE.

qa.q: Who composed the praśasti of Samudragupta?
qa.e: Hariṣheṇa was Samudragupta's court poet.

qa.q: Samudragupta's praśasti was carved on:
qa.e: It was inscribed on the same pillar that carries Ashoka's edicts, now in Prayagraj.

qa.q: Some of Samudragupta's coins show him:
qa.e: These coins suggest he loved music as well as war.

qa.q: Chandragupta II is also known as:
qa.e: Chandragupta II took the title Vikramāditya.

qa.q: Which Chinese pilgrim visited India during Chandragupta II's reign?
qa.e: Faxian came in the early 5th century. Xuanzang came later, in Harsha's time.

qa.q: The famous university at Nālandā is linked with which Gupta ruler?
qa.e: Nālandā is believed to have been founded in the 5th century under Kumāragupta I.

qa.q: Skandagupta is remembered for defending the empire against the:
qa.e: The Hūṇas from Central Asia attacked in the 5th century; Skandagupta pushed them back.

qa.q: Which book did Āryabhaṭa write in 499 CE?
qa.e: The Āryabhaṭīya covers mathematics and astronomy.

qa.q: According to Āryabhaṭa, why do the stars seem to move across the night sky?
qa.a: The Earth rotates on its axis
qa.e: He realised it is the Earth turning that makes the stars appear to move.

qa.q: How did Āryabhaṭa explain eclipses?
qa.a: By the shadows of the Earth and the Moon
qa.e: A solar eclipse is the Moon's shadow on Earth; a lunar eclipse is Earth's shadow on the Moon.

qa.q: Āryabhaṭa's value of pi was about:
qa.e: His value, about 3.1416, is very close to the modern value of pi.

qa.q: Who wrote the Bṛihat Saṁhitā?
qa.e: Varāhamihira's Bṛihat Saṁhitā covers astronomy, weather, plants, gems and more.

qa.q: Why is the Iron Pillar in Delhi famous?
qa.a: It has hardly rusted for more than 1,500 years
qa.e: Its rust resistance shows the great skill of ancient Indian iron-workers.

qa.q: The Iron Pillar stands today in:
qa.e: It stands in the Qutb complex at Mehrauli, Delhi.

qa.q: In which year was India's first satellite, Aryabhata, launched?
qa.e: The satellite Aryabhata was launched in 1975.

qa.q: Who wrote Abhijñāna-Shākuntalam?
qa.e: Kālidāsa wrote this famous Sanskrit play.

qa.q: In Kālidāsa's Meghadūta, who carries the message?
qa.e: Megha means cloud and dūta means messenger.

qa.q: The Ajanta caves are famous mainly for their:
qa.e: Ajanta's paintings show the Buddha's life and Jātaka stories.

qa.q: In which state are the Ajanta caves?
qa.e: Ajanta is in Maharashtra.

qa.q: The Dashāvatāra temple, one of the early stone temples, is at:
qa.e: The Dashāvatāra temple at Deogarh in Uttar Pradesh is from the Gupta age.

qa.q: Which language was most used for literature and royal inscriptions in the Gupta age?
qa.e: Sanskrit flourished as a language of literature and inscriptions.

qa.q: Many Ajanta paintings were made in which century?
qa.e: Many of Ajanta's best-known paintings date to the 5th century CE.

qa.q: What are Jātaka stories?
qa.a: Stories of the Buddha's earlier lives
qa.e: Jātakas tell of the Buddha's past lives and teach good values.

qa.q: What is meant by 'sacred geography'?
qa.a: A network of places in the land that people regard as holy
qa.e: Sacred geography is how people see rivers, mountains, forests and towns as holy and connected.

qa.q: A protected patch of forest linked to a local deity is called a:
qa.e: Sacred groves are forest patches that communities protect because they are sacred.

qa.q: In Kerala, sacred groves are called:
qa.e: Kāvu is the Kerala name; devrai is the Maharashtra name.

qa.q: Which mountain is sacred to Hindus, Buddhists and Jains?
qa.e: Mount Kailash in Tibet is revered by several traditions.

qa.q: The Narmada parikramā is:
qa.a: A pilgrimage walking along both banks of the Narmada
qa.e: Pilgrims walk along one bank to the sea and return along the other.

qa.q: How have sacred groves helped nature?
qa.a: People do not cut trees or hunt there by tradition
qa.e: Belief and tradition protect plants and animals in sacred groves.

qa.q: Which of these trees is widely respected as sacred in India?
qa.e: The peepal is honoured in many Indian traditions; the Buddha attained enlightenment under one at Bodh Gaya.

qa.q: Sacred groves called 'orans' are found in:
qa.e: Orans are community-protected sacred lands in Rajasthan.

qa.q: The word 'tīrtha' originally meant:
qa.a: A ford or crossing place on a river
qa.e: A tīrtha was a crossing place; it came to mean a sacred place of pilgrimage.

qa.q: Which of these is one of the Char Dhām?
qa.e: The Char Dhām are Badrinath, Dwarka, Puri and Rameswaram.

qa.q: Which Char Dhām lies in the west of India?
qa.e: Dwarka is on the coast of Gujarat in the west.

qa.q: How many Jyotirliṅgas are there in the well-known tradition?
qa.e: There are twelve Jyotirliṅgas spread across India.

qa.q: Which city is NOT a site of the Kumbh Melā?
qa.e: The four Kumbh sites are Prayagraj, Haridwar, Ujjain and Nashik.

qa.q: About how often is the Kumbh Melā held at the same site?
qa.e: Each of the four places hosts the Kumbh roughly once every 12 years.

qa.q: The Pandharpur Wārī ends at the temple of:
qa.e: Warkaris walk to the Vitthala (Vithoba) temple at Pandharpur in Maharashtra.

qa.q: How did pilgrimages help unite India?
qa.a: People from different regions travelled and met at shared sacred places
qa.e: Long journeys brought together people of many languages, foods and customs.

qa.q: Where did the Buddha attain enlightenment?
qa.e: The Buddha attained enlightenment under a peepal tree, the Bodhi tree, at Bodh Gaya in Bihar.

qa.q: The Buddha gave his first sermon at:
qa.e: His first teaching was given at Sarnath near Varanasi.

qa.q: Lumbini, the birthplace of the Buddha, is in present-day:
qa.e: Lumbini is in southern Nepal, close to the Indian border.

qa.q: The Shatruñjaya hills at Palitana are sacred to:
qa.e: Palitana in Gujarat has hundreds of Jain temples on its hills.

qa.q: The great statue of Bāhubali (Gommateshwara) is at:
qa.e: The statue stands on a hill at Shravanabelagola in Karnataka.

qa.q: What is the langar at the Golden Temple?
qa.a: A free community kitchen serving meals to all
qa.e: Everyone is welcome to eat together, whatever their background.

qa.q: The dargāh of Khwāja Moinuddin Chishtī is in:
qa.e: This famous Sufi shrine is in Ajmer, Rajasthan.

qa.q: What does the sharing of sacred places by people of different faiths show?
qa.a: A spirit of respect and coexistence
qa.e: Visiting shrines of other faiths reflects India's long tradition of mutual respect.

qa.q: Which of these is a job of a government?
qa.e: Governments make laws, keep order, protect the country and provide services.

qa.q: In a monarchy, the head of state is:
qa.e: A monarch, a king or queen, heads the state in a monarchy.

qa.q: How does a ruler usually get power in a monarchy?
qa.a: By inheriting it in the family
qa.e: Monarchy is usually hereditary: power passes from parent to child.

qa.q: In a constitutional monarchy:
qa.a: The monarch's powers are limited and an elected parliament makes laws
qa.e: A constitution limits the monarch, and elected representatives make the laws.

qa.q: Which country is a constitutional monarchy?
qa.e: Japan has an emperor with a ceremonial role and an elected parliament. India, France and the USA are republics.

qa.q: In an absolute monarchy, who holds most of the power?
qa.e: The king or queen holds almost all power and is not chosen by the people.

qa.q: Why do governments differ from one another?
qa.a: They differ in who holds power and how rulers are chosen
qa.e: The key differences are who rules, how they are chosen and how much say people have.

qa.q: Ancient Indian gaṇas like the Vajji were different from monarchies because:
qa.a: Power was shared by a group meeting in an assembly
qa.e: In gaṇas, many leaders discussed and decided matters together.

qa.q: In a democracy, rulers are chosen by:
qa.e: Democracy means rule by the people, who choose leaders through elections.

qa.q: India is a:
qa.e: Indian citizens elect representatives who make laws on their behalf.

qa.q: What is the minimum voting age in India?
qa.e: Every citizen aged 18 or above can vote.

qa.q: Universal adult franchise means:
qa.a: Every adult citizen has the right to vote
qa.e: All adult citizens can vote, regardless of religion, caste, gender, wealth or education.

qa.q: Which body conducts elections in India?
qa.e: The Election Commission organises and supervises elections.

qa.q: National Voters' Day is celebrated on 25 January because:
qa.a: The Election Commission was set up on that date in 1950
qa.e: The ECI was formed on 25 January 1950, a day before the Constitution came into force.

qa.q: Who said democracy is 'government of the people, by the people, for the people'?
qa.e: Lincoln, a US President, said this in a speech in 1863.

qa.q: In a direct democracy:
qa.e: Citizens decide laws directly, as in ancient Athens.

qa.q: In a dictatorship, the ruler:
qa.a: Holds power without free and fair elections
qa.e: A dictator rules without being freely chosen and usually without accepting criticism.

qa.q: Rule by a small group of powerful people is called:
qa.e: 'Oligo' means few: oligarchy is rule by a few.

qa.q: A theocracy is a government where:
qa.a: Religious leaders rule or laws follow one religion's rules
qa.e: In a theocracy, religion is the basis of the government's power.

qa.q: Which is a key feature of democracy?
qa.a: Rulers can be changed peacefully through elections
qa.e: Peaceful change of government through voting is central to democracy.

qa.q: Which question helps us compare types of government?
qa.e: How rulers are chosen, and whether people have rights, tells us the type of government.

qa.q: In which type of government is freedom of speech best protected?
qa.e: Democracies protect rights like freedom of speech through laws and courts.

qa.q: A government where power passes from parent to child is:
qa.e: Hereditary rule is the mark of a monarchy.

qa.q: Why do democracies have courts and a free press?
qa.a: To protect people's rights and keep rulers accountable
qa.e: Courts and a free press help check misuse of power.

qa.q: When did the Constituent Assembly first meet?
qa.e: The Assembly's first meeting was on 9 December 1946.

qa.q: Who chaired the Drafting Committee of the Constitution?
qa.e: Dr Ambedkar led the committee that prepared the draft.

qa.q: Who was the President of the Constituent Assembly?
qa.e: Dr Rajendra Prasad presided over the Assembly and later became India's first President.

qa.q: On which day was the Constitution adopted?
qa.e: It was adopted on 26 November 1949, now celebrated as Constitution Day.

qa.q: Republic Day, 26 January, marks the day when:
qa.a: The Constitution came into force in 1950
qa.e: On 26 January 1950, the Constitution came into force and India became a republic.

qa.q: About how long did it take to make the Constitution?
qa.e: From December 1946 to November 1949: nearly three years of debate and drafting.

qa.q: How many women were members of the Constituent Assembly?
qa.e: Fifteen women, including Sarojini Naidu and Hansa Mehta, were members.

qa.q: What is a constitution?
qa.a: The basic rulebook of a country
qa.e: It sets up the government, divides powers and protects citizens' rights.

qa.q: With which words does the Preamble begin?
qa.e: It begins 'We, the people of India', showing that power comes from the people.

qa.q: Which two words were added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment in 1976?
qa.e: 'Socialist' and 'secular' were added in 1976.

qa.q: 'Secular' in the Preamble means:
qa.a: The State treats all religions equally and has no official religion
qa.e: A secular State respects all religions equally and does not favour any.

qa.q: India is called a 'republic' because:
qa.a: The head of the state is elected
qa.e: In a republic, the head of state is chosen, not born into the position.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT one of the four values Justice, Liberty, Equality and Fraternity?
qa.e: The Preamble promises justice, liberty, equality and fraternity, not wealth.

qa.q: 'Fraternity' means:
qa.a: A feeling of brotherhood and sisterhood among all
qa.e: Fraternity is the spirit of togetherness that assures dignity and unity.

qa.q: 'Sovereign' means that India:
qa.a: Makes its own decisions without outside control
qa.e: A sovereign country is independent and decides its own internal and external matters.

qa.q: The Preamble promises liberty of:
qa.a: Thought, expression, belief, faith and worship
qa.e: Liberty in the Preamble is about freedom of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship, within the law.

qa.q: How many Fundamental Rights does the Constitution list today?
qa.e: There are six: Equality, Freedom, against Exploitation, Freedom of Religion, Cultural and Educational, and Constitutional Remedies.

qa.q: Which Fundamental Right did Dr Ambedkar call the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution?
qa.e: Without the right to go to court, other rights could not be protected.

qa.q: Fundamental Duties were added to the Constitution in:
qa.e: They were added by the 42nd Amendment in 1976.

qa.q: Which of these is a Fundamental Duty?
qa.e: Protecting public property is a duty; the others are rights.

qa.q: The Right against Exploitation protects children from:
qa.a: Being made to work in factories and hazardous jobs
qa.e: Children below 14 cannot be employed in factories, mines or hazardous work.

qa.q: In which case did the Supreme Court say that the basic structure of the Constitution cannot be changed?
qa.e: In the Kesavananda Bharati case, the Court ruled that Parliament cannot change the basic structure.

qa.q: Which statement about India's Constitution is correct?
qa.a: It is the longest written constitution in the world
qa.e: It is very detailed and is the longest written constitution; it can be amended, but not its basic structure.

qa.q: If a person's Fundamental Right is violated, they can:
qa.e: The Right to Constitutional Remedies lets citizens approach the courts.

qa.q: What is barter?
qa.a: Exchanging goods or services directly without money
qa.e: Barter is a direct swap of goods or services.

qa.q: The 'double coincidence of wants' means:
qa.a: Each person must want what the other person has
qa.e: Barter works only when each side wants what the other offers.

qa.q: A shepherd wants to trade one sheep for a small pot of honey. Which problem of barter does this show?
qa.e: A sheep is worth much more than a small pot of honey, and you cannot cut it into parts.

qa.q: Why is it hard to compare values in barter?
qa.a: There is no common measure like money
qa.e: Without money, people must agree how many of one item equals another every time.

qa.q: Which goods are hardest to store for a long time in barter?
qa.e: Perishable goods spoil, so their value cannot be saved for later.

qa.q: Which of these is an example of barter?
qa.a: Giving two kilograms of wheat for a basket
qa.e: Swapping wheat for a basket uses no money.

qa.q: Why did people move from barter to money?
qa.a: Money is accepted by everyone and solves barter's problems
qa.e: Money removes the need for a double coincidence of wants and gives a common measure of value.

qa.q: Does barter still happen today?
qa.a: Yes, sometimes in villages, fairs and between friends
qa.e: Small exchanges without money still happen in many places.

qa.q: Which of these was used as commodity money in India?
qa.e: Cowrie shells were widely accepted in exchange, so they worked as money.

qa.q: India's earliest coins are called:
qa.e: Punch-marked coins, from around the 6th century BCE, had symbols punched onto metal.

qa.q: Punch-marked coins were mostly made of:
qa.e: Most punch-marked coins were silver.

qa.q: The word 'rupee' comes from the silver coin 'rupiya' issued by:
qa.e: Sher Shah Suri issued the silver rupiya in the 16th century.

qa.q: Which country first used paper money?
qa.e: Paper money was first used in China.

qa.q: Some of the world's earliest coins were made in Lydia, which is in present-day:
qa.e: Lydia was in western Anatolia, in today's Turkey.

qa.q: Which ruling dynasty of ancient India is famous for its gold coins?
qa.e: Gupta kings issued many beautifully designed gold coins.

qa.q: Why does a paper note have value even though paper itself is cheap?
qa.a: People and the government trust and accept it
qa.e: Its value comes from trust and from the government's backing.

qa.q: Which organisation issues currency notes in India?
qa.e: The RBI issues currency notes; the Government of India issues coins and the ₹1 note.

qa.q: When was the Reserve Bank of India set up?
qa.e: The RBI began working on 1 April 1935.

qa.q: In which year was the ₹ symbol adopted?
qa.e: The ₹ symbol was adopted in 2010.

qa.q: The ₹ symbol combines the Devanagari letter 'र' with:
qa.e: It blends 'र' and 'R', with two lines at the top.

qa.q: Prices of goods are written in rupees. Which function of money is this?
qa.e: Money measures how much things are worth.

qa.q: UPI was launched in:
qa.e: UPI was launched in 2016 and is now very widely used.

qa.q: Which is the safest habit with digital payments?
qa.a: Never share your PIN or OTP with anyone
qa.e: Your PIN and OTP are like keys to your money; keep them secret.

qa.q: Who issues coins in India?
qa.e: Coins are issued by the Government of India and distributed through the RBI.

qa.q: What is a market?
qa.a: Any place or arrangement where buyers and sellers exchange goods and services
qa.e: A market can be physical or online; what matters is that buyers and sellers meet to exchange.

qa.q: A weekly haat is:
qa.a: A market held on a fixed day of the week
qa.e: Haats come up on a particular day in a village or town.

qa.q: A market where goods are sold in large quantities to traders is called a:
qa.e: Wholesalers sell in bulk to retailers and other traders.

qa.q: A market with only one seller is called a:
qa.e: 'Mono' means one: a monopoly has a single seller.

qa.q: A market controlled by a few big sellers is called an:
qa.e: 'Oligo' means few: an oligopoly has a few sellers.

qa.q: Why are goods often cheaper at a weekly haat?
qa.a: Sellers do not pay rent for permanent shops
qa.e: Low costs for sellers mean lower prices for buyers.

qa.q: Which is an example of a competitive market?
qa.a: A vegetable market with many sellers
qa.e: Many sellers offering similar goods compete on price and quality.

qa.q: Buying a book through a shopping app is an example of:
qa.e: Online markets let buyers and sellers trade over the internet.

qa.q: Who is a consumer?
qa.a: A person who buys goods or services for use
qa.e: Consumers buy and use goods and services.

qa.q: Wholesalers and retailers who stand between producers and consumers are called:
qa.e: They link producers to consumers, transporting and selling goods.

qa.q: What does MRP stand for?
qa.e: MRP is the highest price at which a product may be sold to a consumer.

qa.q: Which mark should you look for on honey and spices?
qa.e: AGMARK is the quality mark for agricultural products.

qa.q: A gold necklace with the BIS Hallmark tells you:
qa.a: Its gold purity has been certified
qa.e: The Hallmark certifies the purity of gold and silver jewellery.

qa.q: Which law protects consumer rights in India today?
qa.e: The Consumer Protection Act, 2019, sets out consumer rights and how to seek remedies.

qa.q: Which number can consumers call for the National Consumer Helpline?
qa.e: 1915 is the National Consumer Helpline. 108 is for ambulances and 1098 is the child helpline.

qa.q: Why do intermediaries add to the final price of goods?
qa.a: They have costs like transport and storage and need to earn too
qa.e: Each person in the chain adds their costs and earnings to the price.

qa.q: According to the law of demand, when the price of a good rises:
qa.a: People usually buy less of it
qa.e: Higher prices usually reduce the quantity demanded.

qa.q: According to the law of supply, when prices rise, sellers usually:
qa.e: Higher prices mean more profit, so sellers supply more.

qa.q: The price at which quantity demanded equals quantity supplied is called the:
qa.e: At equilibrium price, buyers and sellers agree on the quantity.

qa.q: A mango seller finds that people buy 50 kg a day at ₹40 a kg, 35 kg at ₹60, 20 kg at ₹80 and 10 kg at ₹100. How many kg are bought at ₹60 a kg?
qa.e: The data shows 35 kg are bought at ₹60.

qa.q: A mango seller finds that people buy 50 kg a day at ₹40 a kg, 35 kg at ₹60, 20 kg at ₹80 and 10 kg at ₹100. How many fewer kg are bought at ₹100 than at ₹40?
qa.e: 50 kg − 10 kg = 40 kg fewer.

qa.q: After a very large onion harvest, what usually happens to onion prices?
qa.e: When supply is much larger than demand, prices fall.

qa.q: Why do flower prices often go up just before a big festival?
qa.e: More buyers want flowers at the same time, pushing prices up.

qa.q: A shopkeeper buys 10 kg of rice at ₹45 per kg. How much does she pay?
Which is one of the earliest known farming villages in the Indian subcontinent?
qa.e: Mehrgarh, near the Bolan Pass, shows very early farming of wheat and barley.

qa.q: Which crops were grown at Mehrgarh?
qa.e: Early farmers at Mehrgarh grew wheat and barley.

qa.q: Remains of a ploughed field from Harappan times were found at:
qa.e: Kalibangan in Rajasthan shows a ploughed field with furrows.

qa.q: Who built the Kallaṇai (Grand Anicut) across the Kaveri?
qa.e: The Chola king Karikāla built it about 2,000 years ago.

qa.q: The Kṛiṣhi-Parāshara is an ancient text about:
qa.e: It gives advice on rain, seeds, ploughing and cattle care.

qa.q: The Green Revolution of the 1960s mainly increased the production of:
qa.e: High-yielding wheat and rice varieties greatly increased grain harvests.

qa.q: Which states gained most in the early years of the Green Revolution?
qa.e: Punjab and Haryana had good irrigation and adopted the new seeds quickly.

qa.q: Which scientist is closely linked with India's Green Revolution?
qa.e: Dr M. S. Swaminathan led work on high-yielding varieties in India.

qa.q: Kharif crops are sown:
qa.a: With the arrival of the monsoon
qa.e: Kharif crops are sown in June–July when monsoon rains begin.

qa.q: Which is a rabi crop?
qa.e: Wheat is sown in winter and harvested in spring, so it is rabi.

qa.q: Which is a kharif crop?
qa.e: Rice needs a lot of water and is grown in the monsoon season.

qa.q: Watermelon and cucumber grown in the short summer season are:
qa.e: Zaid crops grow between the rabi and kharif seasons.

qa.q: Black soil is especially good for growing:
qa.e: Black soil holds moisture well and is ideal for cotton; it is also called black cotton soil.

qa.q: Why is red soil red?
qa.e: Iron compounds give red soil its colour.

qa.q: The most fertile soil of the Northern Plains is:
qa.e: Rivers deposited fine alluvium across the Northern Plains.

qa.q: Rabi crops are usually harvested in:
qa.e: Rabi crops sown in winter are harvested in spring, around March–April.

qa.q: Which irrigation method saves the most water?
qa.e: Drip irrigation delivers water directly to the roots, wasting very little.

qa.q: Why do farmers in hilly areas make terraces?
qa.a: To create flat steps and stop soil from washing away
qa.e: Terraces slow rainwater and hold soil on slopes.

qa.q: Crop rotation means:
qa.a: Growing different crops on a field in different seasons
qa.e: Changing crops helps the soil recover nutrients.

qa.q: Which crops help restore nitrogen to the soil?
qa.e: Pulse plants help add nitrogen to the soil.

qa.q: Johads are traditional water-harvesting structures of:
qa.e: Johads collect and store rainwater in dry Rajasthan.

qa.q: Which is a challenge faced by many Indian farmers?
qa.a: Small landholdings and dependence on the monsoon
qa.e: Most farmers have small plots and many depend on monsoon rains.

qa.q: What does a Soil Health Card tell a farmer?
qa.a: The nutrients in their soil and what to add
qa.e: It shows the soil's nutrient status and suggests fertilisers or manure.

qa.q: MSP stands for:
qa.e: MSP is the minimum price at which the government offers to buy certain crops.

qa.q: How many countries share a land border with India?
qa.e: Pakistan, Afghanistan, China, Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh and Myanmar: seven.

qa.q: With which country does India share its longest land border?
qa.e: The India–Bangladesh border is the longest of India's land borders.

qa.q: Which Indian state does NOT border Bangladesh?
qa.e: Sikkim borders Nepal, Bhutan and China, not Bangladesh.

qa.q: Which country borders Manipur and Mizoram?
qa.e: Myanmar lies to the east of Manipur and Mizoram.

qa.q: What is the capital of Bhutan?
qa.e: Thimphu is Bhutan's capital; Kathmandu is Nepal's.

qa.q: Which neighbour lies to the north of India, between India and China, and borders Bihar?
qa.e: Nepal lies along India's northern border and touches Bihar.

qa.q: Citizens of which two neighbours can travel to India without a visa?
qa.e: India, Nepal and Bhutan have open borders for their citizens.

qa.q: Which Indian state borders both Nepal and Bhutan?
qa.e: Sikkim lies between Nepal and Bhutan. (West Bengal also touches both.)

qa.q: Which two countries are India's main maritime neighbours?
qa.e: Sri Lanka and the Maldives are across the sea from India.

qa.q: The narrow strip of sea between India and Sri Lanka is the:
qa.e: The Palk Strait separates Tamil Nadu from Sri Lanka.

qa.q: What is the capital of the Maldives?
qa.e: Malé is the capital of the Maldives.

qa.q: The Maldives lies to the south of which Indian island group?
qa.e: The Maldives is south of the Lakshadweep islands in the Arabian Sea region.

qa.q: India's southernmost point is:
qa.e: Indira Point in Great Nicobar is India's southernmost point; Kanyakumari is the southern tip of the mainland.

qa.q: Which Indian state is closest to Sri Lanka?
qa.e: Tamil Nadu faces Sri Lanka across the Palk Strait.

qa.q: Which of these is a way the sea connects India with its maritime neighbours?
qa.e: Ships, fishing boats and sea trade link India with these island countries.

qa.q: Which countries are close to India's Andaman and Nicobar Islands across the sea?
qa.e: The islands lie near Myanmar, Thailand and Indonesia in the Bay of Bengal and Andaman Sea region.

qa.q: Who wrote the national anthems of both India and Bangladesh?
qa.e: Tagore wrote 'Jana Gana Mana' and 'Amar Shonar Bangla'.

qa.q: Where was the Buddha born?
qa.e: Lumbini, in southern Nepal, is the Buddha's birthplace.

qa.q: Which river is called the Padma in Bangladesh?
qa.e: The main stream of the Ganga is called the Padma in Bangladesh.

qa.q: The Brahmaputra is called the Yarlung Tsangpo in:
qa.e: The Brahmaputra begins in Tibet, where it is known as the Yarlung Tsangpo.

qa.q: In which year was SAARC set up?
qa.e: SAARC was founded in Dhaka in 1985.

qa.q: Which faith links India with Sri Lanka, Bhutan and Myanmar in a special way?
qa.e: Buddhism spread from India and is a major faith in these countries.

qa.q: How do neighbouring countries help each other in hard times?
qa.a: By sending relief and rescue teams after disasters
qa.e: Neighbours send food, medicine and rescue teams after earthquakes, floods and cyclones.

qa.q: Which famous temple in Kathmandu is visited by many Indian pilgrims?
qa.e: The Pashupatinath temple in Kathmandu is a major pilgrimage site.

qa.q: Harṣhavardhana's capital for most of his reign was:
qa.e: Harsha moved from Thanesar to Kannauj, which became his capital.

qa.q: Who wrote the Harṣhacharita?
qa.e: Bāṇabhaṭṭa, Harsha's court poet, wrote his biography.

qa.q: Which Chinese pilgrim visited India during Harsha's reign?
qa.e: Xuanzang came in the 7th century and studied at Nālandā. Faxian came earlier, in the Gupta age.

qa.q: The Tripartite Struggle was fought for control of:
qa.e: The three powers fought over Kannauj in the Ganga plains.

qa.q: Which three dynasties fought the Tripartite Struggle?
qa.e: These three powers from the north-west, east and Deccan competed for Kannauj.

qa.q: The Pāla dynasty ruled mainly in:
qa.e: The Pālas ruled the eastern region of Bengal and Bihar.

qa.q: Who founded the university of Vikramashilā?
qa.e: The Pāla king Dharmapāla founded Vikramashilā.

qa.q: What does 'tripartite' mean?
qa.e: 'Tri' means three; three powers took part.

qa.q: The capital of the Chālukyas of Bādāmi was:
qa.e: Vātāpi, today's Bādāmi in Karnataka, was the Chālukya capital.

qa.q: Which Chālukya king stopped Harsha at the Narmada?
qa.e: Pulakeshin II defeated Harsha's attempt to move south.

qa.q: The Aihole inscription was composed by:
qa.e: Ravikīrti, Pulakeshin II's court poet, composed it.

qa.q: The Pallavas ruled from:
qa.e: Kānchīpuram in Tamil Nadu was the Pallava capital.

qa.q: Narasiṁhavarman I, who captured Vātāpi in 642 CE, was also called:
qa.e: He was called Māmalla, 'great wrestler'; Māmallapuram is named after him.

qa.q: The Pañcha Rathas at Mahabalipuram are:
qa.a: Temples cut out of single rocks
qa.e: Each ratha is carved from one large rock, in the shape of a temple.

qa.q: Pattadakal, with its group of temples, was built by the:
qa.e: The Chālukyas built the Pattadakal temples in Karnataka.

qa.q: Mahendravarman I was not only a king but also a:
qa.e: He wrote Sanskrit plays.

qa.q: Who founded the power of the Rāṣhṭrakūṭas?
qa.e: Dantidurga overthrew the Chālukyas of Bādāmi in the 8th century.

qa.q: The Kailāsa temple at Ellora was built under:
qa.e: The Rāṣhṭrakūṭa king Kṛiṣhṇa I had it carved.

qa.q: What is special about the Kailāsa temple?
qa.a: It was carved from a single rock
qa.e: It is a monolithic temple, cut out of one huge rock.

qa.q: The Kavirājamārga is an early work in which language?
qa.e: It is an early Kannada work on poetics, from Amoghavarṣha I's court.

qa.q: The Ālvārs and Nāyanārs composed devotional songs in:
qa.e: Their bhakti songs were composed in Tamil.

qa.q: The Nāyanārs were devotees of:
qa.e: Nāyanārs worshipped Shiva; Ālvārs worshipped Vishnu.

qa.q: In 712 CE, Sindh was conquered by Arab forces led by:
qa.e: Muhammad bin Qasim led the Arab conquest of Sindh in 712 CE.

qa.q: Which was the later capital of the Rāṣhṭrakūṭas?
qa.e: Mānyakheṭa (Malkhed in Karnataka) was their later capital.

qa.q: Who built the Bṛihadīshvara temple at Thanjavur?
qa.e: Rājarāja I built it; it was completed around 1010 CE.

qa.q: Rājendra I took the title 'Gangaikoṇḍa Chola' after:
qa.a: His army's expedition to the Ganga region
qa.e: The title means 'the Chola who brought (or took) the Ganga'.

qa.q: Rājendra I sent a naval expedition against:
qa.e: The Chola navy sailed against the kingdom of Shrīvijaya.

qa.q: The Uttaramerur inscriptions are about:
qa.a: How village assembly members were chosen
qa.e: They describe rules and the lot system for village assemblies.

qa.q: In the kuḍavolai system, members were chosen by:
qa.a: Drawing palm-leaf tickets with names from a pot
qa.e: Names were written on palm leaves, put in a pot and drawn out.

qa.q: The Chola bronze Naṭarāja shows Shiva as:
qa.e: Naṭarāja means 'king of dancers'.

qa.q: In which river delta did Chola power rise?
qa.e: Thanjavur lies in the fertile Kaveri delta.

qa.q: Which Chola king ruled from 985 to 1014 CE?
qa.e: Rājarāja I's reign was 985–1014 CE; Rājendra I followed him.

qa.q: Which famous temple in Gujarat did Mahmud of Ghazni attack?
qa.e: Mahmud attacked the Somnath temple in Gujarat around 1025–26.

qa.q: Who wrote the Kitāb-ul-Hind?
qa.e: Al-Bīrūnī studied Sanskrit and wrote about Indian life and science.

qa.q: Which queen defeated Muhammad Ghori near Mount Abu in 1178?
qa.e: Nāikī Devī, ruling Gujarat for her young son, led the victory.

qa.q: Who won the First Battle of Tarain in 1191?
qa.e: Prithvīrāj Chauhān defeated Ghori in 1191.

qa.q: In which year was the Second Battle of Tarain fought?
qa.e: The Second Battle of Tarain took place in 1192, a year after the first.

qa.q: The Delhi Sultanate began in:
qa.e: Quṭbuddīn Aibak began to rule from Delhi in 1206.

qa.q: Mahmud of Ghazni came from a kingdom in present-day:
qa.e: Ghazni is in present-day Afghanistan.

qa.q: Why is Al-Bīrūnī's book useful to historians?
qa.a: It describes Indian sciences, beliefs and customs of the 11th century
qa.e: As a careful observer, he recorded much about Indian society and knowledge.

qa.q: The temples of Khajuraho were built by the:
qa.e: The Chandela kings built Khajuraho's temples in Madhya Pradesh.

qa.q: Belur and Halebidu temples were built by the:
qa.e: The Hoysaḷas of Karnataka built these richly carved temples.

qa.q: Who wrote the Rājataraṅgiṇī, a history of Kashmir?
qa.e: Kalhaṇa wrote it in the 12th century.

qa.q: The Līlāvatī, a book of mathematics, was written by:
qa.e: Bhāskarāchārya (Bhāskara II) wrote Līlāvatī in the 12th century.

qa.q: Basavaṇṇa wrote his vachanas in:
qa.e: Basavaṇṇa's vachanas are short sayings in Kannada.

qa.q: Angkor Wat, dedicated to Vishnu, is in:
qa.e: Angkor Wat was built by Sūryavarman II in Cambodia.

qa.q: Who wrote the Gīta Govinda?
qa.e: Jayadeva's Gīta Govinda is a 12th-century Sanskrit poem.

qa.q: King Bhoja, famous as a scholar-king, belonged to the:
qa.e: Bhoja was a Paramāra king of Dhar in Malwa.

qa.q: Where is the Paradesi Synagogue?
qa.e: It stands in Jew Town, Mattancherry, in Kochi, Kerala.

qa.q: In which year was the Paradesi Synagogue built?
qa.e: It was built in 1568.

qa.q: The Bene Israel Jews lived mainly along the:
qa.e: The Bene Israel settled in villages along the Konkan coast.

qa.q: Which Christian community of Kerala is among the oldest in the world?
qa.e: Syriac Christians of Kerala trace their tradition to the 1st century CE.

qa.q: According to tradition, who brought Christianity to Kerala?
qa.e: Syriac Christian tradition says Saint Thomas reached Kerala in the 1st century CE.

qa.q: Which language did the Cochin Jews speak in daily life?
qa.e: Like their neighbours in Kerala, they spoke Malayalam.

qa.q: Why did many groups come to India in the past?
qa.a: For trade, travel or to find safety
qa.e: Traders, travellers and people seeking safety came and many settled.

qa.q: What did communities like the Cochin Jews and Syriac Christians do after settling?
qa.a: Kept their faith and adopted local language, food and dress
qa.e: They became part of Indian society while keeping their identity.

qa.q: The Parsis originally came to India from:
qa.e: Parsis are Zoroastrians whose ancestors came from Persia.

qa.q: According to Parsi tradition, they first landed at:
qa.e: The Qissa-i-Sanjan tells of their landing at Sanjan.

qa.q: Which of these was a Parsi?
qa.e: The nuclear scientist Homi J. Bhabha was a Parsi, as were Dadabhai Naoroji and Jamsetji Tata.

qa.q: The Cheraman Juma Masjid, believed to be one of India's oldest mosques, is in:
qa.e: It is in Kodungallur, on the Malabar coast where Arab traders came.

qa.q: The Siddis of India are of:
qa.e: Siddis trace their ancestry to Africa.

qa.q: Malik Ambar was a powerful minister of the:
qa.e: Malik Ambar, of African origin, rose to great power in Ahmadnagar.

qa.q: The Armenian Church of Holy Nazareth is in:
qa.e: It was built in Kolkata in 1724.

qa.q: What does the 'sugar in milk' story of the Parsis teach?
qa.a: Newcomers can blend in and enrich society
qa.e: The story is a symbol of peaceful blending and contribution.

qa.q: What does pluralism mean?
qa.a: Many communities living together with respect, each keeping its identity
qa.e: Pluralism celebrates diversity with mutual respect.

qa.q: 'Vasudhaiva Kuṭumbakam' means:
qa.e: It is a Sanskrit phrase meaning the whole world is one family. 'Victory to truth' is Satyameva Jayate.

qa.q: Which of these faiths was born in India?
qa.e: Sikhism, like Hinduism, Buddhism and Jainism, began in India.

qa.q: In which year did the Dalai Lama and many Tibetans come to India?
qa.e: They came to India in 1959.

qa.q: Bylakuppe, a large Tibetan settlement, is in:
qa.e: Bylakuppe is in Karnataka; Dharamshala is in Himachal Pradesh.

qa.q: How does the Constitution protect pluralism?
qa.a: It gives freedom of religion and equality to all citizens
qa.e: Freedom of religion and equality are Fundamental Rights for all.

qa.q: Which is an everyday act of pluralism?
qa.a: Sharing festival food with neighbours of other faiths
qa.e: Small acts of sharing and respect build pluralism.

qa.q: Why is India called 'a home to many'?
qa.a: Many communities, faiths and languages have lived here together for centuries
qa.e: India's long history of welcoming and blending many peoples makes it a home to many.

qa.q: Which of these is NOT one of the four elements of a State?
qa.e: The four elements are territory, population, government and sovereignty.

qa.q: Sovereignty means:
qa.a: The power to make one's own decisions without outside control
qa.e: A sovereign State is independent in its internal and external affairs.

qa.q: What happens when a new government is elected?
qa.a: The government changes but the State continues
qa.e: Only those who run the government change; the State remains.

qa.q: Why is India a republic and not a monarchy?
qa.a: Its head of state, the President, is elected
qa.e: In a republic, the head of state is chosen, not born into the post.

qa.q: The government is best described as:
qa.a: The people and institutions that run the State
qa.e: The government makes, carries out and interprets laws for the State.

qa.q: India is a democracy because:
qa.e: In a democracy, people choose who governs them.

qa.q: In the phrase 'the State of India', the word State means:
qa.e: Here 'State' means the whole country, not a part of it.

qa.q: Which is an example of the government doing its work?
qa.e: Making laws is one of the main jobs of government.

qa.q: Which organ of government makes laws?
qa.e: The legislature, such as Parliament, makes laws.

qa.q: Which organ settles disputes and interprets laws?
qa.e: Courts interpret laws and decide disputes.

qa.q: The executive at the Union level is led by:
qa.a: The Prime Minister and Council of Ministers
qa.e: The PM and ministers run the government and carry out laws.

qa.q: India's Parliament consists of:
qa.a: The President, the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha
qa.e: Parliament has three parts: the President and the two Houses.

qa.q: Keeping the three organs separate so that each can check the others is called:
qa.e: Separation of powers prevents any one organ from becoming too powerful.

qa.q: What are the three tiers of government in India?
qa.e: Union, State and local governments work at different levels.

qa.q: Which body is the lowest tier of the panchayati raj system?
qa.e: The gram panchayat works at the village level.

qa.q: Which amendments gave constitutional status to local governments?
qa.e: The 73rd (panchayats) and 74th (municipalities) Amendments were passed in 1992.

qa.q: Which law lets citizens ask government offices for information?
qa.e: The RTI Act, 2005, gives citizens the right to ask for information.

qa.q: Who is a member of the gram sabha?
qa.a: Every adult voter of the village
qa.e: All adult voters in the village are members of the gram sabha.

qa.q: Why do citizens pay taxes?
qa.a: To fund public services like schools, roads and hospitals
qa.e: Taxes provide money for services that benefit everyone.

qa.q: What can a citizen do if their Fundamental Rights are violated?
qa.e: Courts protect citizens' rights.

qa.q: Which of these shows responsible citizenship?
qa.e: Taking care of public property is a duty of every citizen.

qa.q: Citizens vote in elections for:
qa.a: All three tiers: local, State and Union
qa.e: Citizens elect representatives at panchayat or municipal, State and Union levels.

qa.q: How can a 12-year-old be an active citizen?
qa.a: By staying informed, following rules and keeping surroundings clean
qa.e: Children cannot vote yet, but they can be informed and responsible.

qa.q: Villagers want to know how money for a new well was spent. Which is the best step?
qa.a: File an RTI application or ask in the gram sabha
qa.e: RTI and the gram sabha are ways citizens can hold the government accountable.

qa.q: What is infrastructure?
qa.a: Basic facilities like roads, power and water that a country needs
qa.e: Infrastructure is the network of basic facilities that support all economic and social activity.

qa.q: Which is an example of social infrastructure?
qa.e: Schools and hospitals serve people's health and education: social infrastructure.

qa.q: Which of these is a public good?
qa.e: A street light benefits everyone, and one person's use does not stop another's.

qa.q: Why do governments usually provide public goods?
qa.a: Private companies may not make profits from them, but everyone needs them
qa.e: Since people cannot easily be charged for them, the government uses taxes to provide them.

qa.q: Why is infrastructure called an 'engine of development'?
qa.a: It powers growth in farming, industry, health and education
qa.e: Roads, power and communication let every other activity grow.

qa.q: How does an all-weather road help a farmer?
qa.a: She can take crops to market quickly and get better prices
qa.e: Faster, reliable transport helps farmers sell fresh produce.

qa.q: Which is NOT physical infrastructure?
qa.e: Teachers serve education (social); the others are physical facilities.

qa.q: Who usually pays for public infrastructure like roads and bridges?
qa.e: Taxes paid by citizens fund much of India's infrastructure.

qa.q: On which date did India's first passenger train run?
qa.e: It ran from Bori Bunder (Mumbai) to Thane on 16 April 1853.

qa.q: How long was the route of India's first passenger train?
qa.e: The Bori Bunder–Thane route was about 34 km.

qa.q: The Golden Quadrilateral links which four cities?
qa.e: It connects the four big metro cities in a rough square.

qa.q: The North–South corridor links Srinagar with:
qa.e: It runs from Srinagar in the north to Kanyakumari in the south.

qa.q: Where did India's first metro railway open, in 1984?
qa.e: Kolkata Metro opened in 1984; Delhi Metro came later.

qa.q: Which scheme connects villages with all-weather roads?
qa.e: PMGSY, started in 2000, builds rural roads.

qa.q: What is the aim of the UDAN scheme?
qa.a: To make flights affordable and connect smaller towns
qa.e: UDAN focuses on regional air connectivity.

qa.q: The Chenab Bridge in Jammu and Kashmir is famous as the world's:
qa.e: It is the highest railway arch bridge in the world.

qa.q: Electricity produced from flowing water is called:
qa.e: 'Hydro' means water; dams use flowing water to turn turbines.

qa.q: Which of these is a renewable source of energy?
qa.e: Sunlight does not run out, so solar energy is renewable.

qa.q: Why is solar energy good for the environment?
qa.a: It causes less pollution and does not run out
qa.e: Solar panels make electricity from sunlight without burning fuel.

qa.q: How many digits does an Indian PIN code have?
qa.e: The PIN code, introduced in 1972, has six digits.

qa.q: What is BharatNet's aim?
qa.a: To bring broadband internet to every gram panchayat
qa.e: BharatNet is laying optical fibre to connect villages to the internet.

qa.q: Which is an example of communication infrastructure?
qa.e: Mobile towers carry phone and internet signals.

qa.q: Why should citizens not damage public property like trains and bus stops?
qa.a: Repairs cost public money that could be used for other services
qa.e: Public property is paid for with taxes; damage wastes everyone's money.

qa.q: How does good internet help people in villages?
qa.a: They can use online learning, banking and health services
qa.e: Internet connects villages to services that were once only in cities.

qa.q: What are the two main functions of a bank?
qa.e: Banks take deposits from savers and lend money to borrowers.

qa.q: Why does a bank charge more interest on loans than it pays on deposits?
qa.a: To cover its costs and earn a profit
qa.e: The gap between the two rates is the bank's main income.

qa.q: Which is India's central bank?
qa.e: The RBI is the central bank; the others are commercial banks.

qa.q: Where are the headquarters of the RBI?
qa.e: The RBI's central office is in Mumbai.

qa.q: Why is the RBI called the 'banker's bank'?
qa.a: Other banks keep money with it and it guides them
qa.e: Commercial banks keep reserves with the RBI and follow its rules.

qa.q: A bank pays 5% a year on deposits and charges 10% on loans. On ₹200 lent for one year, what is the bank's earning from the difference?
qa.e: Loan interest = ₹20; deposit interest = ₹10; difference = ₹10.

qa.q: How do banks help the economy grow?
qa.a: They turn savings of many people into loans for farming and business
qa.e: Loans help people start businesses, buy equipment and study.

qa.q: Which of these is a service offered by banks?
qa.e: Banks offer lockers, cheques, cards and online banking.

qa.q: Which account is best for a shop that makes many payments every day?
qa.e: Current accounts are designed for frequent business transactions.

qa.q: Which deposit lets you save a fixed amount every month?
qa.e: In a recurring deposit, you deposit the same amount monthly.

qa.q: A fixed deposit is:
qa.a: A lump sum kept for a fixed period, usually at higher interest
qa.e: An FD locks money for a set time and usually earns more interest than a savings account.

qa.q: Ravi deposits ₹250 every month in an RD for 12 months. How much does he deposit in total?
The Pradhan Mantri Jan Dhan Yojana was launched in:
qa.e: It began in 2014 to bring bank accounts to all families.

qa.q: Why should a borrower take only a loan she can repay?
qa.a: She must repay it with interest
qa.e: Loans have to be repaid with interest; borrowing too much can lead to debt.

qa.q: Which account is meant for individuals to save money and earn some interest?
qa.e: A savings account helps individuals save safely and earn interest.

qa.q: A family borrows ₹10,000 and has repaid ₹6,500. How much is still to be repaid (ignoring interest)?
The money that is deposited or borrowed is called the:
qa.e: Interest is calculated on the principal.

qa.q: What is the simple interest on ₹1,500 at 4% a year for 2 years?
What is the simple interest on ₹2,000 at 6% a year for 1 year?
₹1,000 is invested at 10% compound interest. What is the amount after 2 years?
How much more is compound interest than simple interest on ₹1,000 at 10% for 2 years?
qa.e: CI = ₹210, SI = ₹200, so the difference is ₹10.

qa.q: ₹10,000 is invested at 10% compound interest for 3 years. What is the amount?
Why does money grow faster with compound interest?
qa.a: Interest is earned on earlier interest too
qa.e: Each year's interest is added to the amount, and the next year's interest is calculated on the bigger amount.

qa.q: Why is it wise to start saving early?
qa.a: Compounding has more time to grow your money
qa.e: The longer the time, the bigger the effect of compounding.

qa.q: What is a share?
qa.a: A small part of the ownership of a company
qa.e: Buying a share makes you a part-owner of the company.

qa.q: Which is Asia's oldest stock exchange, started in 1875?
qa.e: The BSE in Mumbai started in 1875.

qa.q: Which body regulates the stock market in India?
qa.e: SEBI protects investors and regulates the stock market. The RBI regulates banks.

qa.q: Why is investing in shares risky?
qa.a: Share prices can go down as well as up
qa.e: Share values change with how companies and markets perform.

qa.q: Someone calls and asks for your OTP, saying they are from the bank. What should you do?
qa.e: Banks never ask for OTPs; such calls are fraud.

qa.q: Which helpline number can be used to report cyber fraud in India?
qa.e: 1930 is the national cyber fraud helpline. 1915 is the consumer helpline.

qa.q: Which of these is a digital payment method?
qa.e: UPI lets you pay instantly from a phone.

qa.q: A message says, 'You have won ₹10 lakh! Click this link and enter your bank details.' This is most likely:
qa.e: Unbelievable offers asking for bank details are common scams.
